title: Wind Resource and Weibull Distribution
text:
The wind-resource calculation converts hourly wind speed and direction into a compact probability model. The wake model uses this distribution to calculate annual energy production, while the hydrogen calculations use the same distribution to weight part-load operating states.
The model retains direction because farm power depends on the alignment between the wind and turbine rows. A single all-direction Weibull distribution would remove that dependency.

title: Wind Resource and Weibull Distribution
text:
Source Basis
The intended source is the Dutch Offshore Wind Atlas (DOWA). The official single-point dataset provides hourly modelled wind information for 2008–2017 on a 2.5 km grid and at heights from 10 m to 600 m. DOWA is based on the HARMONIE-AROME weather model nested in ERA5 reanalysis (Royal Netherlands Meteorological Institute (KNMI) 2018).
The legacy calculation uses the following repository files:

The workbook contains 87,601 consecutive hourly records from 2008-01-01 00:00 to 2017-12-29 00:00. It does not identify the DOWA grid point, extraction height, source filename, dataset version or direction convention. It also ends 72 hours before the official 2008–2017 dataset endpoint. The fitted values below are therefore traceable to the legacy workbook, but the workbook is not yet traceable to a specific DOWA extraction.

title: Wind Resource and Weibull Distribution
text:
Direction Sectors
The legacy fitting script divides wind direction \(\theta\) into twelve 30-degree sectors. The stored label is the lower edge of each sector:
\[
s(\theta)
=30^\circ\left\lfloor
\frac{\theta\bmod 360^\circ}{30^\circ}
\right\rfloor.
\]
Sector \(s=0^\circ\) therefore contains observations from \(0^\circ\) up to, but not including, \(30^\circ\). If \(n_s\) is the number of valid observations in sector \(s\) and \(N_\mathrm{obs}\) is the total number of observations, the direction probability is:
\[
p_s=\frac{n_s}{N_\mathrm{obs}},
\qquad
\sum_s p_s=1.
\]
The legacy model passed these labels directly to the wake model as wind directions, displacing each represented direction by up to 15 degrees from its observations. The current model instead spreads each sector’s probability uniformly across the sector, in equal direction steps centred within it (see Numerical Use).

title: Wind Resource and Weibull Distribution
text:
Conditional Weibull Distribution
Wind speed \(v\) within each direction sector is represented by a two-parameter Weibull distribution with shape \(k_s\) and scale \(c_s\). The location parameter is fixed at zero. The cumulative distribution and probability density are:
\[
F_s(v)
=1-\exp\left[-\left(\frac{v}{c_s}\right)^{k_s}\right],
\]
\[
f_s(v)
=\frac{k_s}{c_s}
\left(\frac{v}{c_s}\right)^{k_s-1}
\exp\left[-\left(\frac{v}{c_s}\right)^{k_s}\right],
\]
where \(v\) and \(c_s\) are in m/s and \(k_s\) is dimensionless. The fitting script estimates \(k_s\) and \(c_s\) by maximum likelihood using scipy.stats.weibull_min.fit with the location fixed at zero.
For a speed bin bounded by \(v_i\) and \(v_{i+1}\), the joint probability of direction sector \(s\) and that speed bin is:
\[
w_{s,i}
=p_s\left[F_s(v_{i+1})-F_s(v_i)\right].
\]
This joint probability is the weight applied to the corresponding wake-aware farm-power or conversion state.

title: Wind Resource and Weibull Distribution
text:
Numerical Use
One joint table of direction and speed states serves wake power, electricity yield and hydrogen production alike, so bin edges, tail treatment and weights are identical everywhere. For a direction step \(\Delta\theta\) that divides the sector width, sector \(s\) contributes the directions \(s+(i+\tfrac12)\Delta\theta\) for \(i=0,1,\dots\), each with probability \(p_s\Delta\theta/30^\circ\). Speeds between cut-in and cut-out are binned in steps \(\Delta v\) and represented by the bin midpoint, with the joint probability \(w_{s,i}\) above. All speeds below cut-in or above cut-out form one zero-power state, so the weights cover the whole year exactly. Each weight times the central annual hours gives the state’s hours.
The article case uses 5° and 0.5 m/s steps. Its wake-affected energy differs from a 1° calculation by -0.08%, and single-turbine energy from these states differs from energy from the hourly records by -0.8% (see the reference case). The hourly speeds are treated as hub-height speeds because the workbook does not record its extraction height.
The legacy model used two different grids (0 to 30 m/s in 0.5 m/s steps for PyWake and 0 to 40 m/s in 0.25 m/s steps for hydrogen), with renormalised probabilities. That duplication is removed.

title: Wind Resource and Weibull Distribution
text:
Outputs
The wind-resource calculation supplies:

the twelve direction probabilities \(p_s\);
the Weibull parameters \(k_s\) and \(c_s\) for each direction;
the wind-speed and direction states evaluated by the wake model; and
the joint probability \(w_{s,i}\) of each state.

Availability, electrical losses and conversion losses are not applied on this page. They are applied after wake-aware farm power has been calculated.






WarningRemaining improvements




Recover the source extraction. Record the exact DOWA grid point, height, source filename, dataset version, timezone and direction convention. Replace the shortened workbook series with the complete selected period or explain the 72-hour difference.
Create a controlled input record. Store the fitted CSV with its fitting-script revision, source-file checksum and fit date so that the parameters can be reproduced without the legacy workbook structure.

Sector alignment, the single probability grid and the check of the Weibull reduction against the hourly record are implemented, as described above.


Until the source extraction is recovered, the table above should be treated as a legacy model input rather than a fully verified site-specific wind resource.

title: Turbine Power Electronics
text:
This page defines the turbine electrical output used to compare electricity export, centralised hydrogen and decentralised hydrogen. The adopted model boundary is the AC output of the grid-side inverter, before the step-up transformer. The generator and generator-side rectifier remain common to all cases; their costs and losses are not removed when comparing architectures.
The transformer is outside the turbine cost and power-output boundary used here. It is usually housed inside the turbine, in the tower or nacelle, but physical location does not determine cost ownership (BVG Associates 2019). Its purchase cost and downstream losses belong to electrical infrastructure; its mass still belongs in the applicable supported-mass and lifting inventory.

  subgraph turbine["Turbine accounting scope"]
    G["Generator"] --> R["Rectifier"]
    R --> D["DC link"]
    D --> I["Grid-side inverter"]
  end

The DC branch replaces the AC path; it is not an additional simultaneous export path. “LV side” identifies the lower-voltage transformer winding relative to the infield grid; it does not prescribe a particular equipment voltage class.

title: Turbine Power Electronics
text:
Power Available to Each Architecture
Required inputs are the turbine power curve at the declared boundary and the inverter and transformer efficiencies. Their specifications and evidence belong to Power Conversion Equipment. No numerical efficiency is independently defined on this page.
For electricity export and centralised hydrogen, the power delivered to the infield grid is:
\[
P_{\mathrm{array,in}}=P_{\mathrm{curve}}\eta_{\mathrm{tr}}.
\]
For decentralised hydrogen, removing the inverter recovers its conversion loss:
\[
P_{\mathrm{DC}}=\frac{P_{\mathrm{curve}}}{\eta_{\mathrm{inv}}},
\qquad
\Delta P_{\mathrm{inv}}=P_{\mathrm{curve}}
\left(\frac{1}{\eta_{\mathrm{inv}}}-1\right).
\]
Here \(P_{\mathrm{curve}}\) is inverter AC output, \(P_{\mathrm{array,in}}\) is transformer output, \(P_{\mathrm{DC}}\) is available DC-link power and \(\Delta P_{\mathrm{inv}}\) is recovered inverter loss, all in kW. \(\eta_{\mathrm{inv}}\) and \(\eta_{\mathrm{tr}}\) are dimensionless output/input efficiencies at the applicable operating point. Division reverses the inverter loss; adding a loss percentage is not equivalent. These expressions assume the same upstream operating point and do not authorise operation beyond the generator, rectifier or DC interface ratings.
The DC Integration page defines the direct connection of the electrolyser to the DC link and its matching and protection conditions. The conservative alternative retains a dedicated stack-side DC/DC converter. In either case, retained interface losses are applied after recovering inverter losses. Neither architecture receives a generator or rectifier efficiency credit.

title: Turbine Power Electronics
text:
Cost Boundary
For comparable per-turbine supply costs in EUR2025, let \(C_{\mathrm{legacy}}\) denote a conventional turbine package that includes the transformer, \(C_{\mathrm{tr}}\) its consistently allocated transformer cost, and \(C_{\mathrm{inv}}\) the separable grid-side inverter cost. Then:
\[
C_{\mathrm{turbine,AC}}=C_{\mathrm{legacy}}-C_{\mathrm{tr}},
\qquad
C_{\mathrm{turbine,DC}}=C_{\mathrm{turbine,AC}}-C_{\mathrm{inv}}.
\]
The AC architectures book \(C_{\mathrm{tr}}\) once under electrical infrastructure. The decentralised architecture does not purchase it. Added DC/DC equipment and changes to protection, cooling and cabling are separate retained costs, not part of the inverter credit. An unknown inverter price is not a zero price.
The turbine cost ledger currently includes the transformer in its calibrated conventional package. Reallocation must use that same calibrated term and preserve the combined AC supply cost; subtracting an unrelated supplier benchmark would change the calibration.

The inverter-output boundary above is the adopted model convention, not a claim that every published turbine curve uses the same measurement point. A curve must identify whether converter and transformer losses are already included.

title: Monopile Foundation Mass and Cost
text:
This page estimates the fabricated mass and supply cost of one monopile foundation. The calculation is intended for early-stage comparison of fixed-bottom offshore wind concepts, before site-specific geotechnical and structural design is available.
The two model inputs are the total mass supported above the foundation and water depth. Turbine rated power is not an input: its structural consequence already enters through the component masses calculated on Wind Turbine Mass and Cost.

text:
Monopile Mass
Monopile design is governed by environmental loads, soil conditions, natural-frequency constraints, fatigue, fabrication limits, water depth, and the mass and loading of the supported structure. Segeren and Diepeveen demonstrate that RNA mass affects monopile dimensions and structural response, but do not provide a universal mass-only sizing law (Segeren and Diepeveen 2014). A site-independent structural calculation is therefore not justified by the available inputs.

title: Electricity and Hydrogen: Comparing Energy Carriers for Offshore Wind, over the entire value chain
text:
This research compares two energy carriers for offshore wind — electricity and hydrogen — by designing a complete energy system around each and placing the results side by side. The carrier is the one choice fixed in advance, deliberately, because it is the variable under study. Everything downstream of that choice is left free: generation, collection, conversion, transport, storage, and delivery are designed as one coupled problem, and each carrier gets the architecture that suits it best rather than the architecture built for the other.
Two things distinguish this from most existing techno-economic work on offshore wind and its carrier options. First, scope of the design variables. Many studies comparing transport methods or conversion routes hold turbine spacing, power density, and layout fixed as inputs. Here they are outputs of the same design problem as everything else, because they are physically coupled to it: export capacity depends on how power is aggregated, which depends on where conversion happens, which depends on spacing, which sets the wake losses that shape the production profile the rest of the chain has to handle. Fixing any one of these while designing the rest quietly fixes an assumption the comparison should instead be free to test. Second, scope of the chain itself. The comparison runs through the full chain to delivery, not to the offshore/onshore interface. Where the demand being served is electrical, reconversion equipment and losses belong on the ledger exactly as much as export cables do. Nothing is compared at a midpoint that happens to flatter one option over the other. What that demand consists of — its composition, location, and timing — is not fixed by the research but specified per scenario, so that the comparison can be drawn for different end-uses on the same transparent terms.
The comparison is deliberately between pure systems. Hybrid configurations, in which both carriers leave the farm side by side, are excluded by design — not because they are implausible, but because the question here is comparative rather than global. The aim is not to find the single best North Sea system; it is to isolate what each carrier’s cost structure does to the optimal design when the system is organized entirely around it. A hybrid would blur exactly the contrast the research is built to expose, and the two pure systems bound the space in which any hybrid would sit.

title: Electricity and Hydrogen: Comparing Energy Carriers for Offshore Wind, over the entire value chain
section: Why efficiency is not the objective
text:
Why efficiency is not the objective
This is not a new problem for engineers. A plant built from locally efficient unit operations is not guaranteed to be the cheapest plant to build and run, which is precisely why process design happens at the flowsheet level, not unit by unit. Offshore energy systems have the same structure, and the carrier question is where it shows up most clearly.
Converting electricity to hydrogen and back loses energy that direct electrification does not. That is the correct, uncontested thermodynamic argument, and nothing here disputes it. What is in question is whether it is the right variable to optimize, as opposed to one cost among several to be weighed. A conversion loss is a cost like any other. It can be outweighed by savings elsewhere in the chain, the same way a less efficient piece of equipment can still be the cheaper one to own if it needs less supporting infrastructure around it.
Widen the accounting to the full chain and both carriers show a side that a production-level comparison can’t capture. Electricity’s costs surface downstream, and they come from more than one place. Transmission infrastructure is priced by peak capacity (€/MW) while revenue is earned per delivered MWh. That mismatch alone pushes designs toward protecting utilization: wider spacing, lower installed density, export links sized below peak generation, curtailment by design. A second, independent driver pushes the same way. Wind production and demand rarely line up in time, and because large-scale electrical storage is expensive, the surplus generated in high-production periods has nowhere economical to go and gets curtailed rather than stored. How large that mismatch is depends on the demand profile the system serves; curtailment is evaluated here against exogenous demand profiles, and results are read as conditional on them, with sensitivity to their shape part of the analysis. Neither driver requires the other: capacity could be perfectly sized and curtailment would still happen on the mismatch alone, just as it would happen on the capacity mismatch even with perfectly aligned demand. Both are invisible at the farm gate, where a MWh produced and a MWh delivered are treated as the same thing. High efficiency at the wire can coexist with high infrastructure cost per delivered MWh and low spatial yield.
Hydrogen’s costs and benefits both surface downstream, not just its benefits. Conversion losses are immediate and local, exactly where the thermodynamic argument places them, and if the end-use is electrical, a second conversion loss and its equipment show up again at the far end of the chain. None of that is waived. What also shows up downstream, and what a farm-gate comparison structurally can’t see, is cheaper bulk pipeline transport, cheaper large-scale storage, and export capacity that can be added more gradually than electrical capacity typically allows. A comparison drawn at the farm gate registers hydrogen’s losses and registers none of the rest, in either direction, for either carrier.
Efficiency, in other words, is an instrumental variable, not a terminal one. What is terminal is the cost of energy delivered to the end-user and the sea area required to produce it (MWh/km²), and neither outranks the other by default. Cost is the more familiar objective, so it is worth stating plainly why space carries equal weight here rather than trailing behind it as a footnote. The North Sea is not an empty canvas: shipping lanes, fishing grounds, cables, pipelines, defence areas, and nature protection all compete for the same seabed, and the area allocated to wind development is being fixed now, in blocks, for decades. A design that trades a little energy density for a large reduction in €/MWh is a good answer to a cost-minimization problem and can be a poor one where space is the binding constraint. Which of the two binds first is itself an outcome of architecture and carrier choice, not a fixed fact about the wind resource. Rather than collapsing the two into a single number, results are presented as cost–density trade-offs per carrier, so that the balance between them stays visible instead of being decided inside the model.
Whether the most efficient design is also the cheapest and most space-effective one is not something to assume in either direction. It’s the empirical question this research is built to answer.

title: Electricity and Hydrogen: Comparing Energy Carriers for Offshore Wind, over the entire value chain
text:
Research question and expected mechanism

How does the choice of energy carrier alter subsystem-level marginal cost structures, and how does this reshape the economically optimal offshore wind farm design and the achievable energy density (MWh/km²)?

The expected mechanism is this: the optimal design balances the marginal cost of expanding capacity-rated infrastructure (∂C/∂MW) against the marginal value of delivered energy (€/MWh), and the carrier determines where that balance sits. Where capacity expansion is expensive and discrete, the optimum is expected to shift toward utilization preservation at the expense of installed density; where capacity scales gradually, higher density can remain optimal. Energy density would then be an emergent outcome of system design, not a fixed property of the wind resource, and it may differ by carrier. Whether it does, and by how much, is what the comparison is built to show.

title: Electricity and Hydrogen: Comparing Energy Carriers for Offshore Wind, over the entire value chain
section: The comparison: electricity versus hydrogen as the primary carrier
text:
The comparison: electricity versus hydrogen as the primary carrier
The central comparison places two fully worked-out systems side by side, each designed end-to-end around its own carrier:
Electricity as primary carrier. Power is aggregated electrically, transmitted onshore via standardized high-capacity HVDC blocks, and converted downstream where needed. This is the current North Sea planning paradigm, built on centralized aggregation and bespoke offshore platforms.
Hydrogen as primary carrier. Electrolysis takes place at or near each turbine, and hydrogen, not electricity, is the medium in which energy is collected, transported, and stored. Restructuring around the carrier replaces heavy central aggregation with modular, repeatable conversion units (economies of series rather than scale), collection networks that follow pipeline rather than cable logic, and peak formation, reliability, and storage dynamics distributed across many small units instead of concentrated in one platform.
Hydrogen is worth testing not because it is more efficient — it is not — but because of what sits downstream of the conversion: bulk transport by pipeline, storage at large scale, and export capacity added gradually, all far cheaper than their electrical equivalents. The conversion loss is the price paid for that cheaper chain, which is why the version worth comparing is a farm rebuilt around hydrogen’s downstream economics, not electrolysers added to an electric one.
Each system is designed on its own terms. Neither carrier is evaluated inside an architecture built for the other, which is the comparison this research is designed to avoid.

title: Electricity and Hydrogen: Comparing Energy Carriers for Offshore Wind, over the entire value chain
text:
Method
The comparison is implemented as an integrated techno-economic model of the full chain, from wind resource to delivery. Rather than searching for a single mathematical optimum, the model calculates a wide range of designs for each carrier — varying spacing, conversion siting, export sizing, storage, and the other design variables together — across scenarios for wind climate, distance to shore, institutional block sizes, demand profiles, and financing. The aim is to map where the good designs lie for each carrier and how that map shifts as conditions change, not to pin down a precise best point. Robustness is judged by whether those qualitative patterns persist across the scenario range, not by point-estimate precision.
Market dynamics and price formation are outside the scope: the framing throughout is that a given demand is met at the lowest total system cost. This excludes revenue-side effects — such as the value of selling into high-price hours — for both carriers symmetrically, and keeps the comparison a question of infrastructure cost rather than market behaviour.
The dissertation is deliberately model-first rather than papers-first: the subsystems are so tightly coupled (spacing → wakes → production profile → conversion sizing → export sizing → cost → back to spacing) that isolated component studies would require freezing exactly the variables the research treats as free. The integrated model is the engine from which the papers derive.

title: Electricity and Hydrogen: Comparing Energy Carriers for Offshore Wind, over the entire value chain
text:
Why this matters now
Investment and planning decisions for offshore energy infrastructure are being made now, on multi-decade horizons, under the working assumption that architecture is close to fixed and only production-level parameters remain to be optimized. If that assumption doesn’t hold — if the coupling between spacing, conversion siting, export sizing, and carrier choice materially changes the optimal design — the cost of finding out late is high: offshore infrastructure is expensive to redo and effectively impossible to change once built. Putting the two carriers on equal footing, each with the system that suits it best, and making the comparison explicit and testable now rather than leaving it implicit, is what this research is for.

title: Turbine and Foundation Installation
text:
This page calculates the base offshore installation CAPEX of monopile-supported wind turbines. Installation is divided into two independently scheduled campaigns:

foundation transport and installation; and
turbine transport and erection.

Each campaign is calculated from the number of locations, vessel loads, port distance, installation time and vessel rate. Component masses are used only to check vessel payload and lift feasibility. They are not converted directly into installation time or cost.

Turbine capacity is used to report installation cost per megawatt. It does not directly determine installation duration.
The installation model is architecture-agnostic. Electrical or hydrogen architecture is resolved upstream in the turbine-system calculation and affects this page only through the resulting physical masses. Architecture is therefore not a separate installation input or cost multiplier.
The turbine-system calculation also provides blade, rotor and RNA masses. The baseline calculation does not require RNA mass as an additional input because it is already included in both the nacelle and complete-turbine mass ledger. Introducing it again would double count the same physical change. Blade, rotor and RNA masses become separate installation inputs only if a later installation concept models their transport or preassembled lifts explicitly.
Consequently, a higher-capacity or heavier turbine can increase installation cost when its complete mass reduces the number of sets carried per load. Conversely, an architecture that removes equipment from the nacelle can reduce installation cost when the resulting lower complete-turbine mass avoids a vessel trip. The effect is discrete: if both designs remain within the same payload and lift limits, this simplified model reports the same installation cost.

Turbine campaign
The complete transported turbine-set mass is:
\[

The reference value represents the demonstrated or contractor-specified deck, rack, stability and access limit. Mass can reduce this value but cannot increase it.
For example, a vessel might have sufficient payload for eleven turbine sets but only enough blade racks and usable deck area for six. In that case, \(k_T=6\).

k_{\mathrm{payload},F}

title: Turbine and Foundation Installation
text:
Lift Feasibility Checks
The simplified model applies two coarse lift checks:
\[
m_\mathrm{nacelle}\leq SWL_T,
\]
\[
m_\mathrm{MP}\leq SWL_F.
\]
The nacelle is used as the known turbine lift check because tower-section masses are not yet calculated. The monopile is used as the governing foundation lift.
Passing these checks indicates only that the selected vessel configuration is plausible. It does not prove detailed feasibility because crane capacity also depends on lift radius, rigging, boom clearance and operating conditions.
If either check fails, the campaign is reported as infeasible with the selected vessel assumptions. Selecting and pricing a replacement vessel remains an unresolved project input; no class-based price uplift is inferred.

title: Turbine and Foundation Installation
text:
Initial Evidence Basis
The first version uses three evidence packages.

NREL ORBIT
NREL’s ORBIT methodology provides the campaign structure and port-task assumptions (Nunemaker et al. 2020). Its maintained example configuration provides provisional vessel rate, mobilisation and transit-speed inputs (National Laboratory of the Rockies, n.d.).
For a monopile with a separate transition piece, ORBIT assumes 12 h of monopile fastening and 8 h of transition-piece fastening:
\[
t_{\mathrm{port},F}
=
\frac{12+8}{24}
=
0.833\ \mathrm{day/foundation}.
\]
For one tower set, one nacelle and three blades:
\[
t_{\mathrm{port},T}
=
\frac{4+4+3(1.5)}{24}
=
0.521\ \mathrm{day/turbine}.
\]
The current generic vessel proxy is USD 400,000/day, equivalent to approximately EUR2025 363,297/day after U.S. CPI-U escalation and conversion with the ECB 2025 annual-average exchange rate (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics 2026b, 2026a; European Central Bank 2026). This follows the common financial basis. ORBIT also provides a 7-day mobilisation input and a 10-knot vessel speed:
\[
10\ \mathrm{kn}
\times1.852\ \mathrm{km/nmi}
\times24\ \mathrm{h/day}
=
444\ \mathrm{km/day}.
\]
These are planning-model proxies, not contractor quotations.


South Fork foundation installation
The South Fork Construction and Operations Plan gives approximately 2–4 days per monopile foundation under 24-hour working without weather or sea delay (South Fork Wind, LLC 2021).
The initial foundation parameter is therefore:
\[
t_{\mathrm{site},F}
=
3.0\ \mathrm{days/foundation},
\]
with 2 and 4 days/foundation used as sensitivity cases.
This produces a normal, no-delay foundation estimate. It is not an expected weather-inclusive commercial schedule.


Sofia installation logistics
Sofia provides reference logistics for large modern turbines:

three foundations per vessel cycle (RWE Offshore Wind GmbH 2024); and
six complete 14 MW turbine sets per load (Sofia Offshore Wind Farm 2026).

These are project-specific reference values. They cannot be combined automatically with the generic ORBIT vessel rate because the physical vessel class and commercial rate boundary may differ.
The Sofia values are used as logistics anchors and later validation evidence, not universal defaults.

title: Financial and Price-Basis Assumptions
text:
Canonical Monetary Basis
All costs entering a common model result are expressed in constant 2025 euros (EUR2025). Each imported cost retains its source currency, source price year and cost boundary.
A value with an unresolved price year cannot be adopted as an EUR2025 model input. It may be shown only as a non-combinable reference until the evidence gap is resolved.
No generic geographic, offshore or market multiplier is applied. Such a factor may be introduced only where evidence defines its scope and prevents overlap with component, installation or commercial allowances.

US-dollar escalation to 2025 uses the U.S. CPI-U annual averages as the documented consumer-price fallback, because no single cost-specific index covers the mixed equipment scopes involved (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics 2026). The annual averages are 258.811 (2020), 292.655 (2022) and 321.943 (2025; eleven months, as BLS published no October 2025 value), giving financial-usd-escalation-2020-2025 = 1.24393 and financial-usd-escalation-2022-2025 = 1.10008. text:
This encyclopedia documents the methodology and techno-economic assumptions used to model offshore wind infrastructure, electricity export, offshore hydrogen production, and hydrogen transport.
The site is organised as an assumptions manual. Each component page bundles the modelling choices that matter for that component:
The emphasis is deliberately methodological. Results, scenario outcomes, and interpretation of model output are out of scope for this encyclopedia.
For why this comparison is being made and what question it is designed to answer, see Positioning.

title: Hydrogen Production
text:
Hydrogen production covers the entire electrolyser. A PEM electrolyser is always assumed in this work.
The electrolyser is split up in the following components:

Stack
Power Electronics
Balance of Plant (BOP)

Note that in most contexts, the balance of plant includes the power electronics, but here they are explicitly treated separately.
The compressor is also not included in this section, but is under Hydrogen Infrastructure: Compressor
The hydrogen production model is dynamic: stack efficiency and auxiliary power consumption depend on operating point, which depends on the wind state and the installed stack capacity.
Finally, note that the exact electrolyser composition depends on the system architecture, with the main difference between central and decentral hydrogen production being the power electronics.

title: DC Integration
text:
The decentralised-hydrogen architecture directly couples a wind-turbine generator to a PEM electrolyser through a shared DC system. The model uses this configuration to remove conversion equipment that is only required for AC export or for supplying a conventional AC-fed electrolyser. The feasibility basis is the Hygro technical assessment of direct DC PEM-wind coupling (Verbist and Damen 2026).
The modelled electrical chain is:
wind-turbine generator -> active rectifier/up-chopper -> DC link -> PEM stack or stack array
The architecture has no AC export connection, turbine grid-side inverter, electrolyser rectifier, or separate electrolyser-side DC/DC converter. The generator-side active rectifier/up-chopper remains part of the turbine and controls generator current, electromagnetic torque, and the power extracted from the rotor.

title: DC Integration
text:
The decentralised-hydrogen architecture directly couples a wind-turbine generator to a PEM electrolyser through a shared DC system. The model uses this configuration to remove conversion equipment that is only required for AC export or for supplying a conventional AC-fed electrolyser. The feasibility basis is the Hygro technical assessment of direct DC PEM-wind coupling (Verbist and Damen 2026).
The modelled electrical chain is:
wind-turbine generator -> active rectifier/up-chopper -> DC link -> PEM stack or stack array
The architecture has no AC export connection, turbine grid-side inverter, electrolyser rectifier, or separate electrolyser-side DC/DC converter. The generator-side active rectifier/up-chopper remains part of the turbine and controls generator current, electromagnetic torque, and the power extracted from the rotor.

title: DC Integration
text:
Compared Electrical Cases
Turbine Power Electronics defines the adopted inverter-output power-curve boundary. Both turbine-level cases omit the grid-side inverter: available DC-link power is obtained by dividing that curve output by inverter efficiency, and the separable inverter purchase cost is deducted from turbine cost. Specifications remain owned by Power Conversion Equipment. The supplied curve’s boundary and numerical credit remain unresolved; this relationship must not be applied to an unreconciled generator-output curve.
The article compares three agreed electrical cases. Equipment duty, ratings, costs, losses and evidence gaps for each role are owned by Power Conversion Equipment.

Agreed electrical comparison cases.







Case
Electrical chain
Status




Centralised hydrogen
Conventional turbine electrical chain (generator-side converter, DC link, grid-side inverter, step-up transformer), 66 kV AC collection and a central transformer–rectifier package
Reference comparison


Conservative turbine-level (conservative)
Turbine generator-side converter and DC link, then a dedicated stack-side DC/DC interface
Uses established conversion equipment


Direct DC (converter_reduced)
Turbine generator-side converter and DC link connected directly to the stack array; no dedicated stack-side converter

The generator-side converter is common to all three cases and stays in the common turbine baseline. The rest of this page develops the direct-DC case; the conservative case keeps the dedicated converter, so the feasibility conditions below do not apply to it.






NoteModel assumption



A dedicated electrolyser-side DC/DC converter is not treated as a fundamental requirement. Its functions are instead allocated to generator power control, generator-stack electrical matching, supervisory operating limits, and coordinated protection. This is an integrated turbine-electrolyser design assumption, not an off-the-shelf equipment configuration.

title: DC Integration
text:
Operating Principle
The generator-side converter controls the electrical power supplied to the PEM system. The PEM polarisation characteristic then establishes the corresponding DC voltage and current. For a single stack, or the equivalent polarisation curve of the active stack array, the operating point satisfies:
\[
P_{\mathrm{gen}}
=
V_{\mathrm{stack}}\!\left(I_{\mathrm{stack}}\right)
I_{\mathrm{stack}}.
\]
where:

\(P_{\mathrm{gen}}\) is the generator electrical power supplied to the DC system, in W;
\(I_{\mathrm{stack}}\) is the total current through the active stack configuration, in A; and
\(V_{\mathrm{stack}}(I_{\mathrm{stack}})\) is the voltage given by its polarisation curve at the applicable temperature, pressure, hydration state, tolerance, and age, in V.

As generator power rises or falls, the operating point moves along the applicable polarisation curve. The DC-link voltage is therefore an operating result rather than the primary controlled variable. Voltage is still measured for operating-envelope supervision, converter limits, and protection, but normal hydrogen production does not require a fixed DC-voltage reference.
This distinction replaces the previous page assumption that an active-front-end voltage loop must hold the DC link at a prescribed value. Even where an active rectifier is used, its normal control objective in this architecture is generator current, torque, and power.

title: DC Integration
text:
Model Calculation
At each operating point, the turbine power command is bounded by the available wind power, generator capability, and the power that the PEM system can safely accept:
\[
P_{\mathrm{cmd}}
=
\min\!\left(
P_{\mathrm{wind,available}},
P_{\mathrm{gen,max}},
P_{\mathrm{PEM,permitted}}
\right).
\]
All four terms are powers in W. The permitted PEM power is a supervisory limit derived from current density, stack temperature and pressure, gas purity, water supply, cooling capacity, and the active stack configuration.
The electrical operating point is then found by solving:
\[
P_{\mathrm{cmd}}
=
V_{\mathrm{stack}}\!\left(I_{\mathrm{stack}}\right)
I_{\mathrm{stack}}
\]
within the permitted current and voltage range. The resulting \(I_{\mathrm{stack}}\) and \(V_{\mathrm{stack}}\) are passed to the PEM stack model to calculate hydrogen production, efficiency, and degradation.
If a modular stack array is used, branch switching changes the equivalent polarisation curve and provides coarse capacity selection. Generator torque remains the continuous power actuator.

title: DC Integration
text:
Allocation of Converter Functions
Removing the separate stack converter does not remove its required functions. It reallocates them across the integrated system.

title: DC Integration
text:
Feasibility Conditions

Electrical Matching
The full PEM polarisation envelope must remain within the generator-side voltage and current ratings. The check must cover generator speed, stack temperature and pressure, manufacturing tolerance, and ageing. Matching is achieved through the generator winding design, converter range, series cell count, and any stack-array series/parallel configuration.


Boost-Only Constraint
If the generator-side power stage can only raise voltage, the passive rectified generator voltage must remain below the required stack voltage across the permitted speed range. A design that violates this condition would require a buck-capable conversion stage or a different generator-stack match.


Coordinated Control
The PEM controller must provide a continuously updated permitted-power limit. The turbine controller then applies the lowest of available wind power, generator capability, and this PEM limit. Communication failure must lead to a defined safe state rather than continued operation on a stale limit.


Modular Stack Option
A modular array may improve low-load operation, availability, and maintainability. Branch switching can select the active capacity in discrete steps, while generator torque control adjusts power continuously. Modularity is beneficial but is not a prerequisite for the underlying direct-coupling principle.


Start, Stop, and Faults
Turbine current reduction, pitch control, braking, and electrical isolation must be coordinated with PEM start permissives, stack isolation, purge, and safe shutdown. The control design must define timing and authority for start-up, normal stopping, load rejection, communication loss, and emergency shutdown.


Harmonics and Drivetrain Effects
Diode rectification can introduce generator-current harmonics and electromagnetic torque ripple. Generator electromagnetic design, converter thermal loading, and drivetrain loads therefore require validation for the selected topology (Andresen et al. 2025).






WarningUnresolved design input



The repository does not yet provide the project-specific generator winding voltage, speed envelope, rectifier/up-chopper limits, or PEM polarisation envelopes over temperature, pressure, tolerance, and ageing. Until those inputs are available, the model can define the operating-point calculation and equipment boundary but cannot report a verified matched operating envelope.

title: DC Integration
text:
Evidence Base

Direct Proof of Principle
Clarke et al. directly coupled a 2.4 kW photovoltaic array to a PEM electrolyser without an intervening MPPT unit or DC/DC converter. Series-parallel configurations were selected to match the source and electrolyser voltage-current characteristics, and the system accumulated approximately 600 operating hours. This demonstrates that deliberate electrical matching and the PEM polarisation characteristic can establish a stable operating point without an intervening converter (Clarke et al. 2009).
This is proof of the electrical principle, not direct evidence for a multi-megawatt wind turbine.


Wind-Specific Proof of Principle
Chantharasenawong et al. investigated direct coupling of a fixed-pitch, variable-speed aerogenerator to PEM electrolysers without intervening voltage-conversion or maximum-power-point-tracking electronics. The remote-area system is not representative of a modern offshore turbine, but it directly supports matching a wind generator and PEM load (Chantharasenawong et al. 2008).


Industrial Architecture Support
ITM Power and Ørsted proposed placing an electrolyser at an individual Type IV wind turbine and connecting it directly to the turbine DC link. They identify fewer conversion steps, lower losses, a smaller electrolyser footprint, and removal of AC rectification as potential benefits. The publication also states that the system had not been demonstrated in practice, so it supports the intended architecture but does not prove this exact converter arrangement at scale (ITM Power and Ørsted 2020).


Adjacent Electrochemical Precedent
Fraunhofer ICT’s RedoxWind project connects a redox-flow battery directly to the intermediate DC circuit of a 2 MW wind turbine, eliminating an additional conversion step. A battery is not electrically or operationally identical to a PEM electrolyser, but the project validates turbine-level integration of an electrochemical system on a shared DC circuit (Fraunhofer Institute for Chemical Technology ICT, n.d.).


Engineering Qualification
Recent DC wind-turbine research confirms the potential benefit of fewer conversion stages but generally retains high-power DC/DC conversion for voltage adaptation, isolation, and fault handling. This shows that a DC/DC converter may be useful; it does not show that one is inherently required to determine the PEM operating point. The same work identifies current harmonics and torque ripple as validation topics for diode-rectifier concepts (Andresen et al. 2025).

title: DC Integration
text:
Validation Priorities

Verify the matched generator and PEM voltage-current range over speed, temperature, pressure, tolerance, and ageing

Demonstrate generator-power control against the PEM polarisation model, including low-load transitions and branch switching where used

Component-level turbine and PEM qualification remains necessary but is not repeated here. The new work is the matching, exchange of limits, timing, and allocation of control authority across the shared interface.

title: DC Integration
text:
Model Implication
For the direct-DC case (converter_reduced), the model therefore:

retains the generator-side active rectifier/up-chopper and its losses;
excludes the turbine grid-side inverter and AC export equipment from the hydrogen power path;
excludes an electrolyser rectifier and separate electrolyser-side DC/DC converter;
determines stack voltage and current from generator power and the active PEM polarisation curve; and
retains supervisory controls, measurement, protection, isolation, and balance-of-plant interlocks as required functions.

No converter CAPEX or conversion-loss allowance should be assigned to a separate electrolyser-side DC/DC stage in this case. This treatment applies only if the project-specific electrical matching and protection requirements can be met.
For the conservative case (conservative), the dedicated stack-side DC/DC converter is included, with its cost in conservative-conversion-unit-cost and its efficiency in conservative-conversion-efficiency. Both remain unresolved; candidate evidence and gaps are on Power Conversion Equipment. In both turbine-level cases the removed grid-side inverter and step-up transformer are reconciled against the turbine baseline on Wind Turbine Mass and Cost.






ImportantFinal assessment



Direct DC coupling of a wind-turbine generator and PEM electrolyser without a dedicated electrolyser-side DC/DC converter is technically credible. The turbine controls generator power, while the PEM polarisation characteristic establishes the corresponding DC voltage and current. The remaining gap is full-scale engineering validation, not proof of the underlying electrical principle.

title: Pipeline Pressure and Capacity
text: Pipeline diameter, inlet pressure, and the number of parallel pipelines are not independent choices. They are three different ways of buying the same thing — hydrogen transport capacity — and each buys it through a different cost centre: pipe material, compressor equipment and energy, or installation. This page sets out how those three costs interact and why the resulting optimum is not smooth.

title: Pipeline Pressure and Capacity
text: Pipeline diameter, inlet pressure, and the number of parallel pipelines are not independent choices. They are three different ways of buying the same thing — hydrogen transport capacity — and each buys it through a different cost centre: pipe material, compressor equipment and energy, or installation. This page sets out how those three costs interact and why the resulting optimum is not smooth.

title: Pipeline Pressure and Capacity
text:
Two Ways to Add Capacity
For a fixed pipeline, transport capacity increases with both diameter and pressure drop, but not at the same rate. Diameter enters the capacity relation through the cross-sectional area and the flow velocity together, so capacity scales approximately as \(D^{2.5}\). Pressure enters only through the pressure drop under a square root, so its effect is far weaker and subject to diminishing returns (full derivation in Hydrogen Pipelines).
This asymmetry means diameter and pressure are not equally good levers for the same job, and it is why the two behave so differently in the cost model, not just in the capacity model:

Increasing diameter is the more capacity-effective lever, but it is a step change in material commitment. A larger composite pipeline costs more per metre, and above roughly 8 inch the pipe is assumed to lose the reel-lay flexibility that keeps composite installation cheap in the first place (Hydrogen Pipelines). Past that point, diameter is no longer a lever that can be pulled without also changing the installation method and the cost basis that goes with it.
Increasing pressure adds capacity without any new material or route, but it is equipment- and energy-expensive at the compressor: every bar of additional pressure raises compressor CAPEX and adds a recurring electricity cost for the life of the asset (Hydrogen Compressor).

The same capacity requirement can therefore be met by a fatter pipe running at modest pressure, or a narrower pipe pushed harder by a larger compressor. Which is cheaper is not a property of the pipeline alone; it depends on how the pipe’s material-cost curve compares with the compressor’s cost-and-energy curve over the feasible pressure range.

title: Pipeline Pressure and Capacity
text:
Where Installation Cost Enters
Material and compression are not the whole story, because pipeline capacity is delivered in discrete units. A given diameter-pressure combination yields a fixed maximum flow; if peak hydrogen production exceeds it, the model does not fractionally upsize the pipe — it adds another parallel pipeline. That step adds physical pipe length, interfaces, vessel loads and installation passes.
Installation cost still does not scale as a simple EUR/m coefficient. Parallel lines may share engineering, mobilisation and one broader contractor programme, but each additional line increases the physical installation inventory. The current evidence supports one TCP pipeline per actual lay pass; simultaneous installation of several pipelines must not be assumed without supplier and contractor proof (Cable and Pipeline Installation).
The installation subclass is also tied to the diameter decision. It applies only while the selected pipe remains hydrogen-qualified and compatible with its reel, bend, tension, stability and pull-through limits. Crossing one of those limits can change the vessel, connection concept or pipe technology. Pushing diameter up to avoid another parallel line can therefore trade the discrete cost of an additional pass for a different installation subclass.

title: Pipeline Pressure and Capacity
section: The Resulting Trade-off Is Not Smooth
text:
The Resulting Trade-off Is Not Smooth
Because pipeline count is a ceiling function of required capacity, a small change in peak flow, diameter, or pressure can push a design across the threshold where an extra parallel pipeline becomes necessary — or unnecessary. Near that threshold, the marginal cost of “one more unit of capacity” jumps discontinuously: it can mean a small increase in compressor duty on the existing pipelines, or an entire additional pipeline’s material, interfaces, loads and installation passes.
This is why pressure, diameter, and pipeline count cannot be optimised one at a time. Raising pressure to avoid an extra pipeline only pays off if the resulting compressor cost and energy penalty are smaller than that pipeline’s material and subclass-specific installation cost. Conversely, adding a pipeline only pays off if its complete incremental cost is lower than the compressor cost of reaching the same capacity through pressure alone. The three variables have to be searched jointly over a cost landscape with discrete steps rather than solved as a single continuous minimum.

title: Hydrogen Infield Infrastructure
text:
Hydrogen infield infrastructure collects compressed hydrogen from turbine-integrated electrolysers and delivers it to the export-pipeline connection. It applies only to the decentralised hydrogen architecture. The electricity-export and centralised-hydrogen architectures use 66 kV AC infield cables.
This page defines the proposed network topology and the analytical pipeline-length model. Pipeline material, pressure and capacity are covered on Hydrogen Pipelines. Installation is covered on Cable and Pipeline Installation.

title: Hydrogen Infield Infrastructure
text:
Hydrogen infield infrastructure collects compressed hydrogen from turbine-integrated electrolysers and delivers it to the export-pipeline connection. It applies only to the decentralised hydrogen architecture. The electricity-export and centralised-hydrogen architectures use 66 kV AC infield cables.
This page defines the proposed network topology and the analytical pipeline-length model. Pipeline material, pressure and capacity are covered on Hydrogen Pipelines. Installation is covered on Cable and Pipeline Installation.

title: Hydrogen Infield Infrastructure
text:
Proposed Ladder Layout
The proposed network is a ladder. Two longitudinal header pipelines run along opposite sides of the turbine field. Cross-farm pipelines form the rungs. Turbines connect directly to the rung that passes through their row.






Figure 1: Proposed hydrogen infield ladder. The farm outline, numbers of rungs and turbines and the manifold position are schematic.



The layout is used for four reasons:

A 6 inch composite pipeline at 150 bar is assumed to carry about 500 MW of hydrogen on an HHV-equivalent basis. One rung can therefore collect a complete turbine row without the 60–70 MW string limit of a 66 kV AC cable (Project Team 2026).
Each turbine can send hydrogen to either header. Isolation of one local rung or header segment does not automatically isolate every turbine behind that segment.
The regular grid follows the turbine rows and avoids a separate radial route from every turbine to a central platform.
Flexible composite pipe can be supplied in long reeled lengths. This suits repeated infield runs and reduces the number of offshore field joints relative to rigid steel pipe (Project Team 2026).

The topology provides two infield paths, not two independent export systems. Both paths ultimately reach the same export-pipeline interface. Valves, isolation philosophy and the capacity of the remaining path determine whether the redundancy can be used after a fault.

title: Hydrogen Infield Infrastructure
section: Ladder Geometry for the Reference Case
text:
Ladder Geometry for the Reference Case
The geometry follows the common coordinates of the agreed reference case: a rectangle of breadth \(B\) across the dominant wind and length \(L\) along it, with \(n_L\) crosswind rows of up to \(n_B\) turbines. Turbine centres span the rectangle, and the shorter final row is centred.

Rungs follow the crosswind rows. Each rung spans the full breadth between the two headers, so its horizontal length is \(B\).
Headers run along-wind through the ends of the rows. Each spans from the first to the last row, so its horizontal length is \(L\).
Turbine connections: every turbine sits on its row’s rung. The rung is divided into sections between consecutive turbines; in full rows the end turbines lie on the headers, while the shorter final row needs one extension section at each end to reach them.
Tie-ins join the midpoint of each header to the export manifold at the farm centre, running crosswind along the centreline between the two middle rows; each is \(B/2\) long.

The horizontal ladder length, in km, is:
\[
L_\mathrm{ladder}=n_L B+2L+B.
\]

title: Hydrogen Infield Infrastructure
text:
Manifold Boundary and Tie-ins
The export manifold is at the centre of the farm (agreed 25 September 2026). It is the boundary between infield collection and the export pipeline: sections upstream of it belong on this page, and the export route length is measured from it. Each header drains to its midpoint, so both header halves carry at most half of their side’s rows, and a tie-in from each header midpoint carries that header’s flow to the manifold. Figure 1 shows the ladder topology schematically; it places the export interface at an edge and does not show this central tie-in routing.

title: Hydrogen Infield Infrastructure
text:
Model Representation and Healthy-State Flow
The model reads the collection network as explicit sections (see the model guide): each section has its end nodes, vertical length, route allowance, healthy-state flow share, true internal diameter and absolute inlet and outlet pressures. Non-turbine nodes, such as header nodes and the manifold, are listed separately. Every physical section is included, even if its healthy-state flow is zero.
The healthy-state allocation used for the reference case is:

each rung splits at its centre, with half the row flowing to each header; in a row with an odd turbine count, the middle turbine sends half its flow each way;
each header flows from its ends toward its midpoint;
each tie-in carries one header’s flow, half the farm, to the manifold.

All sections carry flow in this healthy state. At rated output, a full row delivers 127.5 MW to each header, the most heavily loaded header section carries 510 MW and each tie-in 1005 MW (electrical input equivalent; hydrogen flow follows from the stack model).
prepare_common_case.py writes the network nodes (common/collection_nodes.csv) and the section geometry with these flow shares (common/collection_sections_geometry.csv). Vertical length is one water depth per turbine end; header nodes and the manifold are on the seabed, and no route allowance is applied. Section diameters and pressures are design inputs of each case, joined to this geometry in the O7 pressure–diameter study; they are not fixed by the geometry.

title: Hydrogen Infield Infrastructure
Hydrogen Infield Infrastructure
section: Flow and Pressure Checks Versus Redundancy
text:
Flow and Pressure Checks Versus Redundancy
Current checks (healthy state). For the supplied sections and flow shares, the model conserves flow at every node, checks that each section’s capacity covers its peak flow at the supplied inlet and outlet pressures, and rejects a pressure rise at a junction without a compressor. The legacy claim that one 6 inch rung at 150 bar carries about 500 MW supports a single row (127.5 MW per row end) and the most loaded header section (510 MW). It does not cover the tie-ins at 1005 MW each, which need a larger diameter, parallel pipe or a higher pressure; that choice belongs to the pressure–diameter study.
Deferred (D3). Fault states, isolation valves, rerouting through the second header and spare capacity are not analysed. The flow allocation above is not solved as a hydraulic loop network, and the model claims no redundancy benefit. The 100% infield-pipeline availability is a modelling convention, not a reliability result.

title: Hydrogen Compressor
text:
The hydrogen compressor raises the pressure of produced hydrogen from the PEM electrolyser outlet pressure to the pressure required by the hydrogen pipeline system.
The compressor is modelled explicitly because the pipeline injection pressure is a decision variable in this research. The model must therefore capture how compressor energy consumption and compressor cost change when the selected outlet pressure changes. This is necessary for the pressure-diameter optimisation of the hydrogen pipeline system.
Compression is included only in the hydrogen architectures. In the centralised architecture, compression takes place on the offshore electrolysis platform before injection into the export pipeline. In the decentralised architecture, compression takes place at turbine level before injection into the infield hydrogen pipeline.
The compressor model includes compressor electricity consumption, motor losses, CAPEX, OPEX and availability. It excludes electrolyser stack costs, electrolyser BOP, hydrogen drying, pipeline CAPEX, pipeline pressure drop and onshore recompression.






NoteWhy Outlet Pressure Is Modelled Explicitly



The compressor outlet pressure is the pipeline injection pressure, one of the optimisation variables in this research. Raising it trades cheaper, higher-capacity pipeline transport against a larger compressor energy and CAPEX penalty; see Pipeline Pressure and Capacity for how that trade-off plays out against pipeline diameter, pipeline count, and installation cost.
A fixed compressor energy value would hide that trade-off from the optimisation. This page therefore develops explicit compressor energy and cost models as a function of inlet pressure, outlet pressure, and hydrogen mass flow, so that the optimisation has something to weigh the pipeline side against. See Compression Energy and Cost Model below.

The important driver is the pressure ratio, not the absolute pressure difference. Compressing hydrogen from 30 bar to 150 bar has a pressure ratio of 5. Compressing from 1 bar to 150 bar has a pressure ratio of 150. This is why the relatively high outlet pressure of PEM electrolysers is important for offshore hydrogen systems.

title: Hydrogen Compressor
text:
Compression Energy
The number of compression stages is determined from the maximum allowable pressure ratio per stage:
\[
N =
\left\lceil
\frac{\ln(p_\mathrm{out}/p_\mathrm{in})}
{\ln(r_\mathrm{max})}
\right\rceil
\]
where \(r_\mathrm{max}\) is the maximum stage ratio, 3.3. The worked example below uses the illustrative reference duty from 30 bar(a) to 150 bar(a).
The actual pressure ratio per stage is:
\[
r_s =
\left(
\frac{p_\mathrm{out}}{p_\mathrm{in}}
\right)^{1/N}
\]
For the reference case of compression from 30 bar to 150 bar:
\[
\frac{p_\mathrm{out}}{p_\mathrm{in}}
=
\frac{150}{30}
=
5
\]
This gives:
\[
N =
\left\lceil
\frac{\ln(5)}{\ln(3.3)}
\right\rceil
=
2
\]
and:
\[
r_s = 5^{1/2} = 2.24
\]
The compressor shaft work per kg of hydrogen is calculated as:
\[
w_\mathrm{shaft} =
\frac{
N \gamma Z_\mathrm{avg} R T
}{
(\gamma - 1) M_\mathrm{H_2} \eta_\mathrm{comp}
}
\left[
r_s^{(\gamma - 1)/\gamma} - 1
\right]
\]
where \(Z_\mathrm{avg}\) is the average hydrogen compressibility factor between inlet and outlet pressure, evaluated from real-gas hydrogen properties via CoolProp at the arithmetic mean of \(p_\mathrm{in}\) and \(p_\mathrm{out}\). The pipeline capacity model uses its own average-pressure relation; neither calculation assumes an ideal gas.
The electrical energy consumption of the compressor is:
\[
e_\mathrm{comp} =
\frac{
w_\mathrm{shaft}
}{
\eta_\mathrm{motor} \cdot 3.6 \cdot 10^6
}
\]
where \(e_\mathrm{comp}\) is expressed in kWh/kg H₂.
The compressor power demand is then calculated from the hydrogen mass flow rate:
\[
P_\mathrm{comp}
=
e_\mathrm{comp}
\cdot
\dot{m}_\mathrm{H_2}
\]
where \(P_\mathrm{comp}\) is in kW when \(e_\mathrm{comp}\) is in kWh/kg H₂ and \(\dot{m}_\mathrm{H_2}\) is in kg/h.
For annual or time-step calculations, total compressor electricity use is:
\[
E_\mathrm{comp}
=
e_\mathrm{comp}
\cdot
m_\mathrm{H_2}
\]
This energy use is treated as a parasitic load in the hydrogen system.

Sensitivity to Outlet Pressure
Compressor energy consumption increases with outlet pressure because the relevant quantity is the pressure ratio:
\[
\frac{p_\mathrm{out}}{p_\mathrm{in}}
\]
The same outlet pressure can therefore have very different compression penalties depending on electrolyser outlet pressure. Compression to 150 bar is a relatively modest duty when hydrogen leaves the PEM electrolyser at 30 bar, but a much larger duty if hydrogen is produced near atmospheric pressure.
Figure 1 shows \(e_\mathrm{comp}\) across the 80-150 bar outlet-pressure range used elsewhere in the model, for electrolyser outlet pressures of 1, 10, 20 and 30 bar.






Figure 1: Compressor electricity consumption as a function of outlet pressure for different inlet pressures.



The curves confirm why PEM outlet pressure matters: at a given pipeline injection pressure, compressing from 1 bar takes roughly three to four and a half times the electricity of compressing from 30 bar, because it is the pressure ratio that drives compression work, not the absolute pressure difference. Each curve also shows small kinks rather than a smooth rise. These come from the discrete number of compression stages, \(N\): as outlet pressure increases, \(N\) occasionally steps up to keep the per-stage pressure ratio within its 3.3 limit, and each step changes the slope of the curve.

title: Hydrogen Compressor
text:
Cost Model
The compressor cost model is based on the Transition Accelerator technical brief on hydrogen compression (Khan et al. 2021). Its high-flow pipeline-compressor correlation gives uninstalled cost as \(3{,}083.3\,(P_\mathrm{comp}/\mathrm{kW})^{0.8335}\) in 2019 Canadian dollars, where \(P_\mathrm{comp}\) is electrical motor input in kW. The brief’s installation factor of 2 is separate and is not included in the compressor purchase cost on this page. Applicability of that high-flow equipment class to small turbine-level duties still needs checking.
After source-year escalation and currency conversion, let \(A\) [EUR2025] be the coefficient of that same uninstalled power law and let \(\alpha\) be the sourced exponent. The model uses:
\[
C_\mathrm{comp}
=
C_\mathrm{comp,ref}
\left(
\frac{P_\mathrm{comp}}
{P_\mathrm{comp,ref}}
\right)^\alpha,
\qquad
P_\mathrm{comp,ref}=15\,\mathrm{kW},
\qquad
C_\mathrm{comp,ref}=A\,15^\alpha.
\]
The agreed 15 kW reference is a convenient normalisation, not an independently priced compressor or a minimum motor size. Because its cost is derived from the same power law, substitution gives \(C_\mathrm{comp}=A(P_\mathrm{comp}/\mathrm{kW})^\alpha\): the reference power cancels and its numerical choice has no effect on any calculated cost. Rounding \(C_\mathrm{comp,ref}\) independently would break this equivalence. The exponent is below one, so larger compressors are cheaper per kW than smaller compressors; this affects the centralised and turbine-level train comparison, whereas the reference point does not.

Normalisation to EUR2025
The brief’s 2019 Canadian-dollar values are themselves converted from US-dollar HDSAM data: escalated with CEPCI and converted at 0.75 US$/C$, the 2019 average (Khan et al. 2021, Table 4.1). The model therefore reverses that stated conversion to recover the 2019 US-dollar basis. It then escalates in US dollars with the producer price index for air and gas compressor manufacturing, and converts at the common 2025 rate (see Financial and Price-Basis Assumptions):
\[
A=a_{\mathrm{CAD},2019}\;x_{\mathrm{USD/CAD},2019}\;
\frac{I_{\mathrm{PPI}}(2025)}{I_{\mathrm{PPI}}(2019)}\;
\frac{1}{FX_{\mathrm{USD/EUR},2025}}.
\]

Escalating the Canadian-dollar figure with a Canadian index and converting from Canadian dollars would apply Canadian price and exchange-rate movements to US equipment data; the chosen route keeps the index in the market of the underlying data, as the price-basis convention prefers. The index covers US producer prices for all air and gas compressor manufacturing, not hydrogen compressors specifically. The installation factor of 2 remains excluded; installation is costed separately.


Applicability to the Evaluated Duties
The brief states no fitted size range. Its worked pipeline example is 50 t/day compressed from 20 to 70 bar with 1,357 kW motor input, and it describes the HDSAM basis as two- and three-stage reciprocating compressor data, later supplemented by a centrifugal design projection (Khan et al. 2021). Central trains are capped at 1000 kW and are close to that example scale. Turbine-level duties are much smaller: about 12.9 kW per MW of stack at full load for 30 to 100 bar(g), or roughly 0.2 MW per 15 MW turbine at that illustrative outlet pressure. Applying the correlation there extrapolates below the only documented example by a factor of about seven; with the sourced exponent, specific cost at 0.2 MW is about 30% higher than at 1 MW.
Unresolved: the underlying vendor data for large reciprocating compressors (Nexant, Inc. et al. 2008, Table 2-18 and Figure 2-21) have not yet been checked for their size range. Until they are, turbine-level compressor cost carries this extrapolation. The 15 kW reference does not resolve the question: it only fixes the normalisation.


Purchase-Cost Reference per Turbine kW
For an illustrative turbine of 15 MW, use full turbine power and nominal stack capacity equal to turbine rating (1× overplanting). The reference pressures are 30 bar(a) to 150 bar(a). Conversion losses are omitted in this illustration. The stack model allocates the available power between stack, BOP and compression using the supplied polarisation curve (Manufacturer G, n.d.) and the shared BOP electricity input. These are illustration choices, not a completed article case or a selected export pressure.
The compressor motor duty follows from hydrogen flow and specific compression energy. Its purchase cost follows from the EUR2025 correlation above and the train-count rule below. For reporting:
\[
c_{\mathrm{comp,turbine}}=\frac{C_{\mathrm{comp,purchase}}}{P_{\mathrm{turbine}}},
\]
where \(C_{\mathrm{comp,purchase}}\) is compressor purchase cost [EUR2025], \(P_{\mathrm{turbine}}\) is turbine rated electrical power [kW], and \(c_{\mathrm{comp,turbine}}\) is purchase cost per turbine kW [EUR2025/kW]. Motor power remains the cost driver; turbine rating is the reporting denominator.

Installation Boundary
The compressor reference reports purchase cost only. The source’s factor of 2 converts purchase cost to installed cost by adding installation labour and parts (Khan et al. 2021, Table 4.1); it is not adopted as an offshore installation allowance here.
For centralised hydrogen, platform yard integration owns equipment placement, fixing, connections and testing, while platform installation owns offshore hook-up and commissioning. Those scopes and their unresolved inputs must be reconciled with compressor installation before adding any factor. For turbine-level hydrogen, the lifting calculation represents equipment transport and lift requirements but does not yet establish compressor integration, connection and commissioning costs.
TODO (O8): define and cost the remaining compressor installation activities for each architecture, counting each activity once. The source factor may be considered as an aggregate assumption only for otherwise uncosted work after its scope and offshore applicability are addressed. Unresolved installation is not free, and the purchase reference is not a complete installed-cost result.


Cost Sensitivity to Outlet Pressure
Figure 2 repeats the reference calculation across the pressures in Figure 1. Each point recalculates hydrogen output, motor duty, train count and purchase cost at the same available turbine power and stack capacity. It uses the adopted EUR2025 correlation, not the former legacy cost anchor. The curves therefore include the stack’s operating response and any train-count steps as well as the pressure dependence of compression energy.






Figure 2: Compressor purchase cost per turbine kW at full turbine power, with 1× stack capacity and no conversion losses. Installation is excluded.





Train Sizing and Architecture Aggregation
At each production location \(j\), the peak electrical motor demand \(P_{\mathrm{peak},j}\) [kW] follows from the simultaneous stack/BOP/compression power balance. Train count and equally shared train duty are:
\[
n_j=\left\lceil\frac{P_{\mathrm{peak},j}}{P_{\mathrm{train,max}}}\right\rceil,
\qquad P_{\mathrm{train},j}=\frac{P_{\mathrm{peak},j}}{n_j}.
\]
For zero compression duty, train count and cost are zero. The adopted bound compressor-train-limit is a modelling assumption on electrical motor input. It limits economies of scale without adding a spare train. The total supply cost is:
\[
C_{\mathrm{comp,total}}=\sum_j n_j C_{\mathrm{comp,ref}}
\left(\frac{P_{\mathrm{train},j}}{P_{\mathrm{comp,ref}}}\right)^\alpha.
\]
Here \(C_{\mathrm{comp,ref}}\) is reference purchase cost [EUR2025], \(P_{\mathrm{comp,ref}}\) is reference motor input [kW], and \(\alpha\) is the central scaling exponent. Centralised production has one farm-level location; decentralised production sizes each turbine location separately. The method is implemented in model/hydrogen_infra/compressor.py.
The reference cost \(C_{\mathrm{comp,ref}}\) is calculated from the normalisation above (compressor-source-*, compressor-usd-escalation-2019-2025 and compressor-reference-motor-power), not entered as a separate value. The reference table and cost figure call the same train-sizing and supply-cost functions as the architecture calculations.


Operating Cost and Availability
Annual O&M is total installed train supply cost times the adopted compressor-opex-rate [fraction/year]. Availability uses the architecture-specific compressor-*-availability [fraction], applied to the production capacity at that location. Both remain unresolved inputs; no distributed maintenance premium is assumed. The component ledger prevents the same outage from being counted again in production availability. Redundancy, failure-state redispatch and spare-train sizing are deferred.

title: Hydrogen Compressor
text:
Pressure Optimisation
Pressure, diameter and parallel-pipeline choices can be compared in separate deterministic scenarios, for the reasons set out in Pipeline Pressure and Capacity: pressure, diameter, material cost, and installation cost all move together, so none of them can be picked in isolation.
The optimisation problem is therefore not:
\[
\min e_\mathrm{comp}
\]
and it is also not:
\[
\min C_\mathrm{pipeline}
\]
A later optimisation could minimise the combined system cost; the current draft evaluates supplied scenarios:
\[
\min_{p_\mathrm{out}, D, n_\mathrm{pipe}}
LCOE
\]
where \(p_\mathrm{out}\) is compressor outlet pressure and pipeline injection pressure, \(D\) is pipeline diameter and \(n_\mathrm{pipe}\) is the number of parallel pipelines.
The optimum can therefore occur at an intermediate pressure. A higher pressure may be justified if it avoids an extra pipeline. A lower pressure may be preferable if the pipeline is already oversized and additional compression provides little transport benefit.

title: Infield AC Cables
text:
Infield, inter-array or array cables form the medium-voltage collection network inside the wind farm. Each radial string carries the output of several turbines to an offshore AC bus. The cables are used by both the electricity-export and centralised-hydrogen architectures; decentralised hydrogen replaces the main array network with hydrogen pipelines.

Accounted elsewhere

Export cable and onshore connection



This page covers cable supply only. Cable-lay vessels, route preparation, burial, pull-ins and other installation activities are costed separately on Cable and Pipeline Installation.






NotePhysical picture: a radial electrical tree



An array string is comparable to a daisy chain. The first cable segment carries one turbine’s output; each following segment carries that turbine plus every turbine farther from the substation. The final segment into the offshore bus therefore carries the greatest current and usually needs the largest conductor.
The reference design is radial: there is one normal path from each turbine to the substation. This is simple and economical, but a fault near the root of a string can disconnect all turbines downstream of it. A ring or meshed network could provide another path, at the cost of more cable and switchgear.

title: Infield AC Cables
section: Why 66 kV Is the Reference Voltage
text:
Why 66 kV Is the Reference Voltage
Moving from 33 kV to 66 kV approximately doubles the transferable power at the same current. That allows more turbine capacity per string, fewer strings and fewer offshore-platform entries. Carbon Trust estimated that the transition could reduce offshore-wind LCOE by about 1.5%, and DNV GL’s TenneT study found a material reduction in cable length for the Dutch Borssele concept (Carbon Trust 2014; DNV GL 2015).
The technology is now demonstrated at commercial scale. Borssele 1 and 2 used three-phase 66 kV copper array cables in two cross-sections over roughly 170–190 km (Nexans 2018). Fixed 66 kV-class submarine cables fall within the scope of IEC 63026, while project design must also address offshore-specific interfaces, installation and mechanical loading (International Electrotechnical Commission 2019; DNV, n.d.).
66 kV should nevertheless be treated as the current reference, not a permanent optimum. Carbon Trust’s later high-voltage-array work considers 132 kV as turbine and plant ratings grow; it reported modelled savings of GBP 32–50 million for a 1,200 MW future plant relative to an equivalent 66 kV system (Carbon Trust 2022).
