The upper end of this range is used as the screening string rating on this page.
Three ratings should not be confused:

ampacity is the maximum continuous current the installed cable can carry without exceeding its allowable conductor temperature;
MVA capacity follows mainly from voltage and current; and
MW capacity is the active-power share after power factor, reactive duty and engineering derating are allowed for.

A 72 MVA cable does not automatically provide 72 MW of usable wind-power transfer.

title: Infield AC Cables
text:
String Capacity Model
For target farm capacity \(P_\mathrm{target}\) and turbine rating \(P_\mathrm{turb}\), the installed turbine count and capacity are:
\[
N_\mathrm{turb}
=
\left\lceil
\frac{P_\mathrm{target}}{P_\mathrm{turb}}
\right\rceil,
\qquad
P_\mathrm{farm}
=
N_\mathrm{turb}P_\mathrm{turb}.
\]
For a selected usable string rating, the number of full turbines that fit on one radial string is:
\[
n_\mathrm{turb/string}
=
\left\lfloor
\frac{P_\mathrm{string}}{P_\mathrm{turb}}
\right\rfloor,
\]
and the minimum number of strings is:
\[
n_\mathrm{string}
=
\left\lceil
\frac{N_\mathrm{turb}}{n_\mathrm{turb/string}}
\right\rceil.
\]
The floor operator in the first equation prevents a fraction of a turbine being assigned to a string. The ceiling operator in the second ensures that a partly filled final string still receives a complete cable, switchgear bay and platform termination. These discrete jumps are why a small change in turbine or string rating can create a noticeable CAPEX step.
This is the same basic capacity logic used by NREL’s ORBIT model (Nunemaker et al. 2020). Final cable selection must also check voltage drop, short-circuit duty, charging current, burial depth, seabed thermal resistivity, conductor temperature, armour losses and post-installation protection.






NoteWorked example: 15 MW turbines



Four 15 MW turbines place 60 MW on a string. Five place 75 MW on it and exceed the 64–66 MW screening range. A nominal 2 GW target therefore requires 134 turbines, giving 2.01 GW installed and:
\[
n_\mathrm{string}=\left\lceil\frac{N_\mathrm{turb}}{n_\mathrm{turb/string}}\right\rceil.
\]
With 4 turbines per string, the result is 34 strings.


Figure 1 shows the resulting discrete string count. A small increase in plant capacity can require a complete additional feeder, switchgear bay, J-tube, pull-in and cable route.






Figure 1: Required 66 kV radial strings for 15 MW turbines and a 66 MW usable string rating.









WarningThe worked array does not fit the reference platform unchanged



TenneT’s 2 GW reference arrangement shows 24 dedicated wind-farm bays plus four universal bays (TenneT 2024). The 34-string worked case therefore needs more terminations than the maximum 28 shown, even if every universal bay is assigned to a feeder. A consistent design must do one or more of the following:

adopt a cable and platform interface rated for at least 75 MW per string, so five 15 MW turbines fit and only 27 strings are required;
add offshore feeder aggregation or another switchgear interface;
move to a higher collection voltage; or
use a project-specific platform layout with more bays.

This interface constraint must be solved before the 34-string cable count and standard 2 GW platform are combined in one cost case.

title: Infield AC Cables
text:
Cable-Length Model
Cable length is calculated from the modelled turbine layout and radial-string topology. Capacity determines the number of turbines and strings; rotor diameter and spacing determine their separation; farm area, aspect ratio and substation position constrain the coordinates. This keeps cable length responsive when any of those design inputs change.
For rotor diameter \(D\) in metres and along-string and cross-string spacings \(s_x\) and \(s_y\) in rotor diameters, the physical spacings are:
\[
d_x=\frac{s_xD}{1000},
\qquad
d_y=\frac{s_yD}{1000},
\]
where \(d_x\) and \(d_y\) are in kilometres. The wind-layout model places \(N_\mathrm{turb}\) turbines inside the farm boundary using these spacings and returns turbine coordinates \((x_j,y_j)\). The gross farm area \(A_\mathrm{farm}\), spacing and turbine count are not independent: the selected coordinates must satisfy both the minimum-spacing rules and the site boundary. The model must flag an infeasible combination rather than silently rescale the spacing.
For an ideal rectangular grid with \(n_x\) turbine positions along the wind direction and \(n_y\) across it, where \(n_xn_y\geq N_\mathrm{turb}\), the occupied grid spans are:
\[
W_\mathrm{grid}=(n_x-1)d_x,
\qquad
H_\mathrm{grid}=(n_y-1)d_y.
\]
These spans, together with boundary margins and exclusions, must fit inside \(A_\mathrm{farm}\). Farm area is therefore a geometric constraint, not an additional cable-length multiplier. A larger boundary changes cable length only when the layout actually spreads the turbine coordinates farther apart.
The string-capacity calculation above partitions the turbines into radial strings with no more than \(n_\mathrm{turb/string}\) turbines. Let \(\mathcal{E}\) be the resulting set of cable connections: one connection from the offshore substation to the first turbine on each string, followed by turbine-to-turbine connections. The horizontal distance of connection \((u,v)\) is:
\[
d_{uv}
=
\sqrt{(x_u-x_v)^2+(y_u-y_v)^2}.
\]
Total pre-route horizontal cable length is therefore:
\[
L_\mathrm{horizontal}
=
\sum_{(u,v)\in\mathcal{E}}d_{uv},
\]
and the screening supply length is:
\[
L_\mathrm{array}
=
(1+r)L_\mathrm{horizontal}
+
L_\mathrm{pull\text{-}in},
\]
where \(r\) is the route allowance and \(L_\mathrm{pull\text{-}in}\) is the total cable length between seabed touchdown points and turbine or platform terminations. It is included as two vertical legs of the water depth \(d_w\) per connection, \(L_\mathrm{pull\text{-}in}=2d_w|\mathcal{E}|\), as implemented in model/electrical_infra/infield_ac_cables.py. This is a screening length: J-tube routing, hang-off height and slack are not resolved separately.
This is the same calculation structure used by ORBIT’s grid-array model: turbine and row spacing define coordinates, cable capacity limits turbines per string, and the model sums the Euclidean distance between successive connection points (Nunemaker et al. 2020).

BOEM’s review of submitted US construction and operations plans gives an additional portfolio average of 1.48 miles, or approximately 2.4 km, of inter-array cable per wind-turbine foundation (Bureau of Ocean Energy Management 2022).

title: Infield AC Cables
text:
OPEX Allowance
Public evidence describes large but infrequent cable failures more clearly than it reports expected annual cable-only expenditure. ORE Catapult’s SPARTA portfolio found cable outages in 7.46% of wind-farm months and in 61% of reporting wind farms, with outage days split approximately equally between array and export cables (ORE Catapult 2022). Its ELECTRODE programme reports an average repair duration of about two months and consequences often above GBP 10 million, but that amount combines repair expenditure and lost generation (ORE Catapult 2023).
These data do not provide an array-only annual failure frequency or a clean split between physical repair cost and lost revenue. An event-based OPEX model is therefore not used. The current relationship is retained as a top-down risk allowance:
\[
C_\mathrm{OPEX}
=
f_\mathrm{OPEX}C_\mathrm{supply},
\]
with \(f_\mathrm{OPEX}=2\%\)/year and a 1–3% sensitivity. At the base cable price, each 100 km of supplied cable has EUR2025 40 million supply CAPEX and therefore a EUR2025 0.8 million annual allowance. The allowance represents inspection and physical repair provision only. Lost generation remains in the availability calculation and must not also be included in OPEX.

title: Infield AC Cables
text:
Reliability and Availability
The current model applies 99.0% array-network availability as a flat annual yield multiplier. A radial string fault normally disconnects the turbines downstream of the fault rather than the complete wind farm, so the flat multiplier does not represent topology explicitly.
No more detailed failure model is introduced until consistent array-specific failure frequency, repair duration and affected-capacity data are available. When those inputs exist, the radial connections \(\mathcal{E}\) defined by the cable-length model can also define the turbines isolated by each fault. Until then, 99.0% remains a transparent aggregate assumption rather than a calculated reliability result.

title: Electricity Export with HVDC
text:
The electricity-export architecture carries electrical energy from each wind turbine to the defined onshore electrical delivery point. Turbine output is conditioned for AC infield collection, aggregated and converted to HVDC on an offshore platform, exported to shore, and converted back to AC at the onshore grid connection.
The physical boundary includes the wind turbines, their support structures, the complete offshore and onshore electrical chain, and the grid-connection interface. It ends where the project hands electrical energy over at the defined onshore electrical delivery point.

title: Component Mapping
text:
Installation and Common Project Scope
Installation is not a physical energy-flow component, but it remains within the economic boundary for every included asset. The Offshore Installation section owns the installation methods and assumptions for turbines, foundations, cables, pipelines, and platforms.
The shared cost schema retains required project categories. Development, shared engineering, insurance and owner contingency are currently unresolved. Construction finance, taxes and financing fees are excluded by the approved simple-CRF convention rather than embedded in component costs.
Wider onshore network reinforcement is excluded unless a scenario explicitly assigns it to the offshore project.

title: Component Mapping
text:
Accounting Rule
Architecture pages determine whether a component or function is included. Component and methodology pages determine how it is represented. A cost, loss, availability factor, installation activity, or replacement is booked by its canonical owner and must not be added again on an architecture page.
Capital and carrier-cost reporting follows System Boundary and Carrier-Cost Metrics.

title: About
text:
This site documents the assumptions behind a component-level techno-economic model for offshore wind infrastructure.
The model compares electricity-based export, centralised offshore hydrogen production, and decentralised turbine-integrated hydrogen production. The documentation here is limited to methodology and assumptions: system boundaries, component cost models, energy balances, availability factors, installation assumptions, and shared financial conventions.
The model is under development. Hover over a sidebar link to see whether each page is context only, not reviewed, blocked, partially implementable, implementable with declared uncertainty, or ready. A section tooltip reports the least-ready calculation page in that section; it is not an editorial-completion percentage.

The source base includes the formal public bibliography and controlled working documents. Public evidence can be checked independently. Internal supplier, manufacturer and project evidence can be reproduced only by authorised readers with access to the controlled source. Where a public fallback, bounded range or sufficient derivation is absent, confidential evidence is not independently reproducible and the affected result remains limited or blocked.
See References and Evidence Status for the access and model-use classification of every catalog record.

title: Centralised Hydrogen
text:
The centralised-hydrogen architecture retains the conventional turbine electrical chain and AC infield collection system. Electricity is aggregated and converted to hydrogen on one integrated offshore platform. Hydrogen is then compressed, exported through a subsea pipeline, and handed over at the defined onshore hydrogen delivery point.
The physical boundary includes the wind turbines and support structures, AC collection, the integrated central platform, compression, pipeline export, and the onshore hydrogen-delivery interface. It ends at that connection; the onshore hydrogen backbone itself is outside the boundary.

  D --> E["Hydrogen compression"]
  E --> F["Hydrogen pipeline export"]
  F --> G["Onshore hydrogen-backbone connection"]

title: Centralised Hydrogen
text:
Integrated Offshore Platform Boundary
The architecture contains one physical offshore platform. The platform integrates:

AC collection and aggregation
electrolyser transformers and rectifiers
PEM stack modules
non-electrical electrolyser balance of plant
seawater intake, desalination, and electrolyser-grade water treatment

Compression is a separate downstream functional and accounting subsystem. It is physically hosted on the same platform but is not included in the electrolyser or balance-of-plant component boundary. This distinction keeps compression cost and energy consumption separate from hydrogen-production equipment.

title: Decentralised Hydrogen
text:
The decentralised-hydrogen architecture converts electrical energy to hydrogen at each wind turbine. Hydrogen rather than electricity is collected within the wind farm, exported through a subsea pipeline, and handed over at the defined onshore hydrogen delivery point.
The physical boundary includes the wind turbines and support structures, turbine-integrated hydrogen-production equipment, turbine-level compression, the infield hydrogen network, export pipeline, and onshore hydrogen-delivery interface. It contains no central offshore conversion platform.

  D --> E["Hydrogen infield collection"]
  E --> F["Hydrogen pipeline export"]
  F --> G["Onshore hydrogen-backbone connection"]

text:

The calculation excludes joints, terminations, operating-temperature effects, return-current imbalance and converter losses. Annual cable loss should be calculated from the time series:

title: Onshore Grid Connection
text:
The onshore grid connection transfers power from the HVDC cable system into the national AC transmission network. It is not one item of equipment. It is an interface chain comprising the shore crossing, underground DC cable, onshore converter station, converter transformers, high-voltage switchgear, protection and control, and the connection to an existing or new transmission substation.
For TenneT’s 2 GW reference, the chain is:

  E --> F["380 kV switchgear"]
  F --> G["National transmission grid"]






The converter station itself is technically described and costed as part of the complete link on HVDC Converter Stations. This page owns the physical grid interface and makes clear which onshore costs remain unresolved.
The point of common coupling (PCC) is the electrical and contractual boundary where the offshore connection meets the transmission system. Physically, the onshore converter lies in the chain on this page. Commercially, its equipment and civil works may belong to the same converter-station package as the offshore station. title: Onshore Grid Connection
text:
Physical Layout
At landfall, the submarine cable is brought ashore through an open trench or, more commonly at sensitive coastlines, ducts installed by horizontal directional drilling. Submarine and land cable designs are connected in accessible transition-joint bays. The separate pole, metallic-return and communication cables then continue underground to the converter site.
The onshore converter changes DC power back to three-phase AC. Converter transformers provide voltage transformation and electrical separation, while reactors, filters and controls manage current, harmonics, voltage and reactive power. High-voltage switchgear connects the station to the transmission grid and isolates equipment for faults and maintenance.
TenneT describes the Dutch 2 GW interface as 525 kV DC conversion to 380 kV AC. Its standard onshore arrangement has six single-phase converter transformers plus one spare (TenneT 2024). For the Doordewind connection, TenneT reports an onshore converter-station footprint of roughly 5.5 ha before the underground connection to the 380 kV substation (TenneT, n.d.). The land requirement reflects electrical clearances, converter halls, cooling, transformers, roads, drainage, security and construction space; it is not just the building footprint.

title: Onshore Grid Connection
text:
Electrical Rating
AC equipment must carry more than active MW alone:

active power \(P\), measured in MW, transfers net energy and is what the wind farm is primarily selling;
reactive power \(Q\), measured in MVAr, oscillates between electric and magnetic fields and is used to control AC voltage; and
apparent power \(S\), measured in MVA, combines both and determines much of the current and thermal loading of transformers, converters and switchgear.

Power factor is \(P/S\). A value below one means some equipment current is being used for reactive rather than active power.
At unity power factor, the AC line current associated with 2 GW at 380 kV is:
\[
I_\mathrm{AC}
=
\frac{P}{\sqrt{3}V_\mathrm{LL}\cos\phi}
=
\frac{2{,}000\times10^6}
{\sqrt{3}(380\times10^3)}
=3.04\ \mathrm{kA}.
\]
The station is not designed as one 3 kA conductor. Power is divided among converter transformer windings, bus sections and grid circuits so equipment ratings, fault levels and maintenance criteria can be satisfied.
Reactive-power operation increases apparent power:
\[
S=\frac{P}{\cos\phi},
\qquad
Q=\sqrt{S^2-P^2}.
\]
If 2 GW were delivered at a power factor of 0.95, the terminal duty would be about 2.105 GVA and 657 MVAr. This is an illustration, not a selected grid-code operating point. Actual reactive capability is specified as a voltage-dependent envelope and can require converter-current headroom, reactors or additional compensation.
The grid-connection study must check at least:

rated and temporary voltage ranges;
active-power ramping and frequency response;
reactive-power and voltage-control capability;
fault ride-through and post-fault active-power recovery;
harmonic emission and resonance;
short-circuit level and protection coordination;
maximum permissible loss of infeed.

Several of these terms describe different questions. Fault level is the current the surrounding grid can supply into a short circuit; it affects switchgear duty and converter-control behaviour, not how often faults occur. Fault ride-through asks whether the link remains connected during a temporary voltage depression. Harmonics are unwanted waveform components that can cause heating, resonance or interference. A strong grid node is one whose voltage and stability remain acceptable when 2 GW changes or trips–not merely one with high annual energy demand.
Commission Regulation (EU) 2016/1447 sets the European HVDC framework for these active-power, reactive-power, voltage, fault-ride-through, control, protection and monitoring capabilities (European Commission 2016). Project-specific requirements are then agreed with the relevant transmission-system operator.
The current Dutch system code adds useful numerical context at the point of connection (Government of the Netherlands 2026):








Requirement

These are compliance limits, not normal operating set points. They should be verified against the code version and connection agreement used for the project; converter MVA, transformer duty and compensation cannot be sized from a single nominal power factor alone.

title: Onshore Grid Connection
text:
Capacity and Connection Architecture
The HVDC link is sized in discrete 2 GW blocks in the reference model:
\[
n_\mathrm{link}
=
\left\lceil
\frac{P_\mathrm{export}}{2{,}000\ \mathrm{MW}}
\right\rceil.
\]
This does not prove that the receiving grid can accept \(2n_\mathrm{link}\) GW at the selected PCC. A grid study determines whether existing 380 kV circuits have sufficient thermal, voltage and stability margin and whether a new substation, busbar extension, underground cable or overhead-line reinforcement is required.
The connection point can therefore drive project economics independently of offshore distance. A shorter sea route to a weak grid node may require more onshore reinforcement than a longer route to a strong node. The model should treat:

dedicated connection assets from landfall to the agreed grid point; and
wider network reinforcement triggered beyond that point

as separate cost categories. Their payer and regulatory treatment may also differ.

title: Onshore Grid Connection
text:
Conversion and Transformer Losses
The current model fills the previously blank onshore efficiency with a provisional aggregate 98.5%. This covers the onshore converter, converter transformers and station auxiliaries once. Hitachi Energy reports conversion losses below 1% per station for the 900 MW DolWin2 VSC system (Hitachi Energy, n.d.), supporting the order of magnitude but not establishing a 2 GW guarantee.
Large-transformer efficiency regulation provides another useful check. For liquid-immersed large transformers, the European Tier 2 minimum peak-efficiency index is 99.770% at 100 MVA, rises with rating and reaches 99.797% at 200 MVA and above (European Commission 2014). Applicability and exclusions must be checked for the selected equipment. PEI is measured at the loading point of maximum efficiency, so it must not be interpreted as constant full-load or annual efficiency.
The project does not yet have the OEM loss curves and auxiliary-load specifications needed for a load-dependent calculation. Until those data are available:

title: Onshore Grid Connection
text:
Availability, Curtailment and Resilience
The internal model assigns 98.0% availability to the onshore station. This is the same onshore-terminal factor documented on the converter-station page and shown in the section overview; it is applied once, not multiplied by a second 98% grid-interface factor. As with the offshore station, a single scalar hides equipment redundancy and degraded states. The standard bipole can retain about 1 GW after a pole-path outage, while a common auxiliary, control, busbar or grid event may remove the complete 2 GW.
Energy-equivalent availability is:
\[
A_E
=
1-
\frac{\sum_i\Delta P_i\Delta t_i}
{P_\mathrm{rated}T}.
\]
A practical state model distinguishes:








State
Export capability
Example

Converter transformer, valve or pole maintenance

0 GW
Shared auxiliaries, busbar or protection event


Receiving grid constrains dispatch
0–2 GW
Congestion, system security or market curtailment



The last state is not equipment unavailability. Grid curtailment should be an energy-system or dispatch constraint so it can be valued and mitigated separately. Planned maintenance, spare single-phase transformers, sectionalised buses, redundant cooling and black-start arrangements can all affect outage duration and residual capacity.

title: Hydrogen Pipelines
text:
Hydrogen pipelines transport compressed hydrogen through the infield collection network and from the wind farm to the onshore hydrogen interface.
The model distinguishes between infield pipelines and export pipelines, but documents them together because the same diameter, pressure, capacity, and material-cost logic applies. The infield topology and length calculation are documented on Hydrogen Infield Infrastructure. Installation is excluded from this page and is documented separately in Cable and Pipeline Installation.
The pipeline model covers:

material CAPEX for composite flexible hydrogen pipelines
transport capacity as a function of diameter, pressure, and route length
the number of parallel export pipelines required for a wind-farm hydrogen flow
the coupling between pipeline pressure, compressor duty, and total LCOE

title: Hydrogen Pipelines
text:
Composite Flexible Pipelines
Composite flexible pipelines are used as the reference hydrogen pipeline technology in this model. A flexible composite pipe typically combines a hydrogen-compatible liner, load-bearing composite reinforcement, and a protective outer layer. Compared with a rigid steel pipeline, the relevant system-level advantage is not only material substitution. The important offshore feature is that the pipe can be manufactured and transported in long continuous lengths, spooled on a reel, and laid with fewer welded field joints.
This matters for offshore hydrogen infrastructure because the model is concerned with many repeated infield connections and, in the decentralised architecture, a pipeline grid that replaces the AC infield cable network. Flexible composite lines are lighter than steel lines at the diameters considered here, are less exposed to corrosion-related design issues, and can simplify installation logistics. These advantages are especially relevant for infield pipelines and for export pipelines up to the diameter range that remains compatible with reel-lay handling.
The flexibility benefit is not unlimited. Larger diameters and higher pressure classes require more reinforcement and increase minimum bend radius. The source material therefore caps the composite export-pipeline diameter at 8 inch: above this range, the pipeline is assumed to lose the reel-lay flexibility that motivates the technology choice (Project Team 2026).

text:
Sizing Variables
Pipeline sizing is governed by the variables in Table 1.



Table 1: Main pipeline sizing variables.









Variable
Role in the model




Internal diameter, \(D\)
Determines cross-sectional area and strongly affects capacity.


Inlet pressure, \(p_\mathrm{in}\)

Outlet pressure, \(p_\mathrm{out}\)

Sets frictional pressure loss for a given flow.

Determine the Fanning friction factor used in the capacity equation.

For the export pipeline, the agreed reference case uses a 100 km physical route and a delivery pressure of 66 bar(g), which is 67.01 bar(a) in the model’s absolute-pressure equations. The delivery level is the upper operating pressure described for the West-Netherlands hydrogen network (Concept Notitie Reikwijdte En Detailniveau 2026), allowing injection without an additional onshore compressor in the base case. Inlet pressure and diameter are design inputs of each case.

Hydrogen Pipelines
Hydrogen Pipelines
text:
Material Cost Model
Pipeline material CAPEX is based on confidential supplier quotes for selected combinations of diameter and pressure class (Supplier S, n.d.). The model uses a fitted bilinear surface over diameter and pressure:
\[
c_\mathrm{mat}(D,p_g)=a+b\,D+c\,p_g+d\,D\,p_g
\]
where \(c_\mathrm{mat}\) is material cost per unit length [EUR2025/m], \(D\) is the diameter [inch], \(p_g\) is the operating pressure [bar(g)], and \(a\), \(b\), \(c\) and \(d\) are confidential coefficients fitted to the quotes. Unlike an interpolation through the quote points, the fit is one smooth surface: it need not reproduce each quote exactly, and it returns values outside the quoted range by extending the same bilinear trend.
Stay within the quoted range. Evaluate cases only for diameters and pressures inside, or at most slightly outside, the quoted diameter and pressure classes. Beyond them, the linear extension has no supplier support and can misstate cost in either direction. The quoted range is not yet recorded in the repository (TODO: record the minimum and maximum quoted diameter and pressure class without disclosing prices). The confidential fit returns material price in EUR2025/m; the project owner confirmed this price basis on 25 September 2026, so the model’s quote-to-EUR2025 factor pipeline-quote-to-eur2025 is 1.
Pressure basis: the fit is read at the section’s operating inlet pressure in bar(g), without a design margin (agreed 25 September 2026). The model converts its absolute pressures by subtracting the standard atmosphere before calling the fit.
Total material cost for a pipeline route is:
\[
C_\mathrm{mat}
=
L
\cdot
c_\mathrm{mat}(D,p)
\]
For multiple parallel export pipelines:
\[
C_{\mathrm{mat},\mathrm{export}}
=
n_\mathrm{pipe}
\cdot
L_\mathrm{export}
\cdot
c_\mathrm{mat}(D,p)
\]
The current cost model covers material cost only. Installation, burial, connection, vessel time, lay-pass grouping and termination work are excluded here and treated in the shared installation section. More than one TCP pipeline per lay pass is not assumed without project-specific evidence.

Confidentiality Handling
The raw supplier quotes and fitted material-cost surface are confidential. They are used only to parameterise the model and are not reproduced in this encyclopedia page. Figures derived from them show pressure and diameter on their true scale, since those are model inputs, not supplier data. The cost axis is left without tick labels so that only the shape of the cost curves, not the underlying price level, is disclosed.


Material Cost vs. Pressure
Figure 2 shows pipeline material cost as a function of inlet pressure, for the same diameters used in Figure 1. Cost increases sharply from one diameter class to the next, which is expected for a larger pipe, but at fixed diameter the increase with pressure is comparatively small. Material cost, in other words, is mainly a diameter decision. It is capacity, not material cost, that responds strongly to pressure, which is why pressure and diameter play such different roles in the trade-off described in Pipeline Pressure and Capacity: raising pressure is cheap on the pipe itself, and its real cost shows up at the compressor instead (Hydrogen Compressor).






Figure 2: Hydrogen export-pipeline material cost as a function of inlet pressure and diameter.





Cost per Unit of Transport Capacity
Figure 3 divides the cost curves in Figure 2 by the capacity curves in Figure 1, giving material cost per unit of transport capacity at each diameter and pressure.
Because capacity scales much more strongly with diameter than material cost does, cost per unit capacity falls as diameter increases. This is the basis for the earlier claim that the economic optimum tends toward the largest feasible composite diameter. The same ratio also falls with pressure, at diminishing rate, for the same reason: on the pipe alone, more pressure buys more capacity for very little extra material cost. This curve reflects material cost only. It does not include the compressor cost and energy penalty that pressure also brings, which is why a pure cost-per-capacity view of the pipeline cannot be used to pick a pressure on its own — see Pipeline Pressure and Capacity for how the compressor side of that trade-off is brought back in.






Figure 3: Hydrogen export-pipeline material cost per unit of transport capacity, as a function of inlet pressure and diameter.

title: Hydrogen Infrastructure
text:
Hydrogen infrastructure covers everything that moves hydrogen from the electrolyser outlet to the onshore interface: compression, and the pipeline network that carries the gas offshore and to shore.
The section is split into:

Hydrogen Infield Infrastructure — ladder topology for the decentralised architecture and the calculation of total infield pipeline length.
Hydrogen Compressor — raises hydrogen from electrolyser outlet pressure to the pipeline injection pressure, with the associated electricity consumption, CAPEX, and OPEX.
Hydrogen Pipelines — composite flexible pipeline technology, diameter and pressure sizing, transport capacity, and material cost, for both the infield network and the export route.
Pipeline Pressure and Capacity — how pipeline diameter, inlet pressure, and installation cost trade off against each other in sizing the pipeline system.

Compressor and pipeline assumptions are coupled rather than independent: higher inlet pressure increases compressor energy consumption and cost but also increases pipeline capacity, which can reduce the number of parallel pipelines required. Pipeline count in turn interacts with installation cost, because a single lay vessel can install multiple pipelines together. Pressure, diameter, and pipeline count are therefore optimised jointly rather than one at a time.
The current hydrogen infrastructure model assumes no additional hydrogen losses in pipelines after compression.

title: Balance of Plant
text:
The balance of plant (BOP) includes the non-electrical auxiliary equipment required to operate the PEM electrolyser stack safely and continuously. In this model, the BOP manages feedwater supply, heat removal, gas-liquid separation, hydrogen drying, hydrogen-side piping, instrumentation and housing.
Because the system is offshore, the feedwater system must also include seawater intake, desalination and final purification to electrolyser-grade water.
Power electronics are excluded completely because the required components depend on the electrical architecture. Transformers, rectifiers and other electrical conversion equipment are discussed on Electrolyser Power Electronics.
The stack, compressors, hydrogen export system, offshore installation, offshore structures and indirect project costs are also represented elsewhere in the model.
The scope used in this page is therefore:

title: Balance of Plant
text:
Cost Basis

Scope of Cost Estimate
The non-electrical BOP cost is based on the NREL PEM electrolyser manufactured cost analysis (Badgett et al. 2024). NREL reports subsystem costs for a 1 MW PEM electrolyser system in 2020 USD per kW of electrolyser capacity (Table 10).
The base case uses the NREL 1,000 MW/year manufacturing-volume case because the offshore hydrogen system considered here represents industrial-scale deployment rather than early low-volume manufacturing.
Electrical BOP is excluded from the NREL cost breakdown. The NREL water supply category is also separated from the generic BOP cost because offshore seawater treatment requires an explicit desalination and purification model.
This page distinguishes between three cost levels:

Cost levels used to interpret the BOP estimate.







Cost level
Meaning
Treatment in this model




Manufactured cost
Factory production cost reported by NREL
Used as the starting point


Equipment purchase cost
Manufactured cost plus manufacturer markup
Used for the BOP reference cost


Installed offshore cost
Equipment cost plus installation, structures, offshore logistics, contingency and indirect costs
Excluded here and represented elsewhere





NREL Reference Cost
The remaining non-water, non-electrical BOP manufactured costs used in the base case are:

Non-water non-electrical BOP manufactured costs from the NREL 1,000 MW/year manufacturing-volume case.






Subsystem
Manufactured cost [2020 USD/kW]




Thermal management

A manufacturer markup of 50% is applied to convert manufactured cost into an approximate equipment purchase cost. The resulting marked-up non-water BOP reference cost is:
\[
c_\mathrm{BOP,ref} = 1.5 \cdot 222 = 333 \ \mathrm{2020\ USD/kW}
\]
For the 1 MW NREL reference system, this corresponds to:
\[
C_\mathrm{BOP,ref} = 333{,}000 \ \mathrm{2020\ USD}
\]
This value excludes power electronics, stack costs, offshore water treatment, installation, offshore structures, site preparation, indirect costs, inflation and offshore-specific cost adders.


Offshore Water Treatment
The purchased treatment package converts seawater into electrolyser-grade water. A study of an electrolyser integrated with an offshore wind turbine reports vendor quotes for reverse-osmosis packages with a second RO pass, cleaning, electro-deionisation and controls. The study states that these packages deliver water at the required electrolyser quality (Chico Moreno 2021, Table 43). Its two complete-package references are:

Vendor-quoted RO and deionisation package references, reported in a 2021 study (Chico Moreno 2021). The €/m³/h values divide package price by package output; they are comparison metrics, not continuously scalable unit rates.








Package
Clean-water capacity
Quoted investment
Unit cost at quoted capacity




Small
100 m³/day = 4.17 m³/h
€0.30 million
€72,000 per (m³/h)


Large
3,800 m³/day = 158.3 m³/h
€3.0 million
€18,900 per (m³/h)



The quotes do not establish the costs of seawater intake, intake screening, stack-water recirculation, offshore installation or additional redundancy. These remain separate unresolved costs. The prices are treated as approximately 2021 euros because the study does not specify the quote dates. No additional manufacturer markup is applied to quoted package prices.
The model treats water treatment as part of the aggregate BOP. Its reference purchase cost at the 1 MW reference capacity, bop-water-reference-purchase-cost (TODO (EUR)), is added to the non-water reference cost and scaled with the same exponent and block rule (see Scaling Method). The quotes above are evidence for choosing that value, not a separate calculation. They cannot be read off directly: at 10 L of clean water per kg H₂ and about 19.6 kg/h per MW of stack input at the 3 A/cm² rating, a 1 MW reference needs about 0.2 m³/h, far below the smallest quoted package (4.17 m³/h). The water reference cost therefore remains an unresolved input.


Scaling Method
Cooling, gas-liquid separation, drying, piping and instrumentation can be shared across multiple stacks. The BOP therefore does not scale linearly with installed capacity. Water treatment is scaled in the same way, as part of the aggregate BOP.
Because the exact scaling exponent is not known, the model uses the six-tenths rule as a first-order process-equipment scaling approximation. The six-tenths rule is a standard preliminary process-equipment cost-scaling method in which cost scales with capacity using an exponent close to 0.6 (Engineering LibreTexts, n.d.; Peters et al., n.d.).
For a BOP unit with capacity \(P_i\), the BOP cost, including water treatment, is:
\[
C_{\mathrm{BOP},i} =
\left(C_\mathrm{BOP,ref}+C_\mathrm{water,ref}\right)
\left(
\frac{P_i}{P_\mathrm{ref}}
\right)^{\alpha}
\]
where \(P_\mathrm{ref}\) is the NREL reference capacity (1000 kW), \(C_\mathrm{BOP,ref}\) the marked-up, escalated non-water reference cost, \(C_\mathrm{water,ref}\) the water-treatment reference purchase cost and \(\alpha\) the scaling exponent (0.6). The total is \(C_{\mathrm{BOP,total}}=\sum_i C_{\mathrm{BOP},i}\).
Each production location is divided into equally loaded BOP blocks:
\[
n_b=\left\lceil\frac{P_{\mathrm{served}}}{P_{\mathrm{block,max}}}\right\rceil,
\qquad P_i=\frac{P_{\mathrm{served}}}{n_b}.
\]
Here \(P_{\mathrm{served}}\) is the wind capacity served at that location [kW], \(P_{\mathrm{block,max}}\) is bop-block-limit [kW], and \(n_b\) is the integer block count. Stack overplanting does not increase this BOP sizing basis. Centralised production shares farm power across its blocks; decentralised production sizes blocks independently at each turbine.
The whole BOP uses bop-scaling-exponent. The block limit is an explicit modelling choice that prevents unlimited centralisation benefits. Lower limits can be evaluated through named scenario overrides. No spare block is included. The method is implemented in model/hydrogen_production/balance_of_plant.py; its cost result remains incomplete while the water reference cost is unset.


Manufacturing Volume Sensitivity
The base case uses the 1,000 MW/year NREL manufacturing-volume case. The 10 MW/year and 100 MW/year NREL cases may be used in sensitivity analysis to represent less mature supply chains or slower industrial scale-up.

Water treatment scales with the same exponent as the rest of the BOP. Water quality, redundancy, offshore intake and installation remain additional design and cost uncertainties.

title: Balance of Plant
text:
BOP Power Consumption
The BOP also consumes electricity during electrolyser operation. This consumption is treated separately from stack electricity consumption.
The BOP power consumption represents parasitic loads from auxiliary systems such as pumps, fans, chillers, recirculation blowers, thermal management and hydrogen drying.
Compression is excluded from this value because compression is represented elsewhere in the model. Electrical conversion losses are also explicitly excluded because power electronics are represented separately.
The NREL report cites a generic BOP electricity consumption of 4.2 kWh/kg H₂ (Table 1), but this value includes electrical losses and is therefore not directly applicable to the non-electrical BOP scope used here (Badgett et al. 2024).
The underlying Ruth and Ahluwalia source (Badgett et al. 2024) separates BOP losses into electrical, mechanical and hydrogen-related losses. After excluding electrical losses, the remaining BOP consumption is:

Non-electrical BOP electricity consumption after excluding electrical losses.








Operating point
Mechanical [kWh/kg H₂]
Hydrogen [kWh/kg H₂]
Total [kWh/kg H₂]




Rated power, BOL
1.3
0.2
1.5


Rated power, EOL
2.3
0.2
2.5


Minimum-loss point, BOL
0.4
0.1
0.5


Minimum-loss point, EOL
0.6
0.1
0.7



A simple lifetime average gives approximately 2.0 kWh/kg H₂ at rated power and 0.6 kWh/kg H₂ at the minimum-loss operating point. The difference is mainly caused by thermal management. At the minimum-loss operating point, the stack operates more efficiently and therefore produces less waste heat. Lower waste heat reduces the cooling duty and associated mechanical power consumption.
In this study, the stack is deliberately oversized so that the electrolyser usually operates closer to the minimum-loss point than to rated stack operation. The model therefore assumes an average non-electrical BOP power consumption of:
\[
e_\mathrm{BOP} = 1.0 \ \mathrm{kWh/kg_{H_2}}
\]
This value includes mechanical BOP loads and hydrogen drying losses. It is selected as a conservative average. It is higher than the minimum-loss values reported by Ruth and Ahluwalia to allow for offshore cooling, water handling, drying, control systems, part-load operation and uncertainty in auxiliary loads.

Desalination
Offshore desalination and water polishing are small compared with the main BOP parasitic loads. A worst-case reverse-osmosis electricity use of 5.0 kWh/m³ corresponds to approximately 0.05 kWh/kg H₂ when 10 L of water is required per kg H₂. This is small relative to the assumed 1.0 kWh/kg H₂ BOP consumption.
Desalination power is therefore included within the BOP power allowance unless a separate water-treatment model is used.
The total BOP electricity consumption is calculated as:
\[
E_\mathrm{BOP} = e_\mathrm{BOP} \cdot m_\mathrm{H_2}
\]
where \(E_\mathrm{BOP}\) is the BOP electricity consumption and \(m_\mathrm{H_2}\) is the hydrogen production.
The assumed value of \(e_\mathrm{BOP}\) should be interpreted as an average value for an oversized offshore PEM electrolyser operating predominantly away from rated stack power.

Model Limitations
This BOP model is intended for early-stage techno-economic assessment. It should not be interpreted as a detailed offshore BOP design.
The main limitations are:

Main limitations of the current BOP model.






Limitation
Implication




Land-based NREL cost data are used as the cost basis
Offshore packaging, redundancy, corrosion protection and maintainability are not explicitly costed


A generic 0.6 scaling exponent is used for the whole BOP
This captures broad economies of scale but not detailed equipment-train sizing


Water treatment scales with the aggregate BOP exponent
Package-size thresholds of water treatment are not represented


Offshore intake and installation costs remain unresolved
The quoted RO/deionisation package costs do not establish complete offshore water-system CAPEX


BOP electricity consumption is represented by a single average value
Dynamic behaviour, thermal transients and detailed part-load operation are not modelled


Compression is excluded
Any compression energy and cost must be added elsewhere in the model



The aggregate scaling approach covers the whole BOP, including water treatment. Offshore intake and installation costs and block-limit sensitivity remain explicit uncertainties.

title: Power Electronics
text:
Electrolyser power electronics convert the 66 kV infield AC supply to the controlled low-voltage DC required by the PEM stacks.
This page represents the complete conversion chain between the 66 kV platform input and the stack DC terminals as one aggregated subsystem. It includes the plant step-down transformer, rectifier transformers, rectifier cabinets, converter controls, and dedicated conversion-system cooling. Turbine-side conversion equipment is covered in Wind Turbine Mass and Cost. The PEM stack and its polarisation behaviour are covered in Stack. Hydrogen compression is covered separately in Compressor.

title: Power Electronics
text:
Reference Architecture
The reference configuration is a water-cooled, 24-pulse thyristor rectifier supplied through a phase-shifting rectifier transformer. Multi-pulse thyristor conversion remains a common industrial solution at multi-megawatt scale because it combines high efficiency, low semiconductor cost, high current capability, and established reliability. Contemporary commercial systems are offered in 6-, 12-, 18-, and 24-pulse arrangements, with harmonic distortion decreasing as pulse number increases (ABB 2025). Reviews of large-scale electrolyser converters likewise identify thyristor rectifiers as the established high-power option, while active-front-end and chopper-based systems trade higher cost and conversion complexity for improved power quality and controllability (Yodwong et al. 2020; Chen et al. 2022).
The 66 kV input is represented as an aggregated two-stage voltage reduction:
\[
66\ \mathrm{kV\ AC}
\rightarrow
\mathrm{medium\mbox{-}voltage\ AC}
\rightarrow
\mathrm{controlled\ stack\ DC}.
\]
The intermediate voltage and detailed transformer winding arrangement are not modelled. Large-plant studies use comparable high-voltage-to-medium-voltage distribution followed by repeated transformer–rectifier modules, including PEM layouts based on approximately 40 MW power blocks (Noordende and Ripson 2020).

title: Power Electronics
text:
Cost Basis
Published power-electronics costs are not fully like-for-like. The literature includes manufactured cost, purchased-equipment cost, and installed system cost, with different transformer and auxiliary-equipment boundaries. Where a source explicitly reports manufactured cost before markup, the same 50% manufacturer markup used for the stack and balance-of-plant costs is applied here before comparison (see Financial and Price-Basis Assumptions), rather than treating any single source as a directly transferable quotation.
NREL adopts a cost of 199 USD/kW for the transformer and rectifier of a 1 MW PEM electrolyser, based on historical supplier quotations and explicitly excluding manufacturer markup, installation, soft costs, and inflation (Badgett et al. 2024). Applying the standard 50% markup gives an equipment purchase cost of:
\[
1.5 \times 199 \approx 300 \ \mathrm{USD_{2020}/kW}
\]
Fraunhofer ISE estimates PEM power-electronics costs of approximately 160 EUR/kW in its 2020 cases and approximately 101–102 EUR/kW in its 2030 cases, reported at the system/investment level rather than as a bare manufactured cost. Its 100 MW cases add a separate high-voltage transformer of approximately 25–26 EUR/kW, giving a combined large-system estimate of approximately 185–186 EUR/kW. The specific cost of the power electronics changes only marginally between the 5 MW and 100 MW cases (Holst et al. 2021). A recent industrial comparison reports substantially lower Chinese-market investment costs for 5 MW packages: approximately CNY 270/kW for a thyristor rectifier including its phase-shifting transformer, compared with CNY 320/kW for a diode-plus-chopper system and CNY 400/kW for an IGBT system (Gao et al. 2025). No CNY-to-EUR conversion is applied here: the comparison is used only to confirm that thyristor rectifiers are the lower-cost topology, not as a quantitative anchor, because the geography, project scope, installation boundary, and procurement conditions differ too much for a direct rate conversion to be meaningful.
No public vendor source was found that provides a binding price for a complete offshore 66 kV-to-DC package with a consistent scope. Vendor literature is therefore used to confirm topology, modularity, and efficiency, but not as the primary cost basis.
A reference value of 185 EUR/kW for the complete purchased 66 kV-to-stack-DC conversion package is taken from Fraunhofer’s combined large-system transformer-plus-power-electronics estimate. It indicates the order of magnitude only; it is not a calculation input. The model’s central-conversion-unit-cost (TODO (EUR/kW)) remains unset until a normalised EUR2025 value is adopted. This sits well below the marked-up NREL benchmark of approximately 300 USD/kW for a small 1 MW reference unit — compared here at face value, pending complete EUR2025 normalisation (see Financial and Price-Basis Assumptions) — and above the lowest reported regional equipment prices.

title: Power Electronics
text:
Cost Scaling
No six-tenths-rule scaling is applied. The subsystem is treated as repeated transformer–rectifier power blocks, giving a scaling exponent of 1.00.
This assumption is based on practical unit limits rather than an assumption that electrical equipment has no economies of scale. Industrial rectifiers operate at very high current and are built from parallel semiconductor devices and repeated bridges because a single device cannot supply the complete plant current (Gao et al. 2025). Commercial high-power converter units are typically limited to the multi-megawatt range, after which plant capacity is increased mainly by adding modules (Chen et al. 2022). Large electrolyser designs similarly number up repeated stack and transformer–rectifier blocks rather than enlarging one converter indefinitely (Noordende and Ripson 2020).
Fraunhofer’s bottom-up results support this approximation: specific power-electronics cost is nearly constant between 5 MW and 100 MW, unlike centralised process equipment that benefits more strongly from shared capacity (Holst et al. 2021). Some plant-level economies can still arise from shared engineering, controls, switchgear, buildings, and procurement. The exponent of 1.00 should therefore be interpreted as a conservative purchased-equipment assumption, not proof that total installed electrical-system cost is perfectly linear.

Energy Balance
For centralised electrolysis, the model applies one net conversion loss between the 66 kV AC input and the stack DC terminals:
\[
P_{\mathrm{stack,DC}}
=
P_{\mathrm{in,66kV}}
\left(1-L_{\mathrm{conversion}}\right).
\]

Net power-conversion assumption for centralised electrolysis.







Parameter
Central assumption
Sensitivity range




Net 66 kV AC-to-stack-DC efficiency
97.5%
96.0–98.5%


Net conversion loss
2.5%
1.5–4.0%



The 2.5% loss includes the plant step-down transformer, rectifier transformers, rectifier semiconductor losses, and dedicated conversion-system cooling. It does not include infield cable losses, general platform auxiliaries, or stack electrochemical losses.
The value represents a modern, high-efficiency thyristor package rather than a generic historical fleet average. ABB reports rectifier-only efficiency of up to 99.6% for its current water-cooled thyristor product (ABB 2025). An industrial comparison reports thyristor rectifier efficiency above approximately 98.5% and complete transformer-plus-rectifier efficiency above 97.5% (Gao et al. 2025). Fraunhofer assumes rectifier efficiencies of 96% for its 2020 design and 98% for its 2030 design, with a separate high-voltage transformer efficiency of 99% (Holst et al. 2021). The selected 97.5% net value is therefore representative of an efficient contemporary package while retaining losses for the full 66 kV-to-DC chain.
A constant net loss is used at all plant loads. In practice, efficiency depends on loading, transformer no-load losses, firing angle, cooling demand, and current ripple. Multi-pulse conversion and modular dispatch reduce, but do not eliminate, these effects. The loss sensitivity should be used where the annual operating profile contains substantial low-load operation.

Availability
Transformer and rectifier outages are included in the overall electrolyser availability factor and are not applied as an additional derating on this page.
The physical system is expected to consist of multiple conversion blocks, so failure of one block may cause partial rather than complete plant unavailability. Explicit block redundancy, spare strategy, failure rates, and offshore repair logistics are outside the current model resolution.

title: Stack (PEM)
text:
The PEM electrolyser stack is the primary energy conversion component of the hydrogen production system. It converts electrical power and water into hydrogen and oxygen and therefore largely determines the overall efficiency of the electrolyser.
Within this model, the stack is represented explicitly because its efficiency, degradation and sizing have a strong influence on the optimal design of the offshore energy system. Rather than optimising the stack in isolation, it is evaluated as one component of the complete offshore hydrogen production chain.
PEM stacks are present in both centralised and decentralised hydrogen production architectures.






NoteWhy PEM?



PEM electrolysis is selected because it is well suited to variable renewable electricity. The technology can rapidly follow fluctuations in wind power while maintaining high efficiency over a wide operating range.
Another important advantage is that hydrogen is produced at an elevated outlet pressure (approximately 30 bar in the source material), reducing the required downstream compression ratio compared with low-pressure electrolysis technologies.
See the Compressor page for more discussion.

title: Stack (PEM)
text:
Stack Model
The stack model consists of four interacting components:

stack efficiency
modular operation
degradation
cost

Together these determine the optimal installed stack capacity and operating strategy.

title: Stack (PEM)
text:
Polarisation Curve
Engineering principle
The electrical energy required to produce hydrogen depends on the cell voltage. As current density increases, the cell voltage rises because activation, ohmic and mass transport losses become larger. Consequently, stack efficiency decreases at higher current densities.
Model implementation
Stack efficiency is calculated from a manufacturer polarisation curve (Manufacturer G, n.d.) relating cell voltage to current density. The operating point is defined as a percentage of the maximum current density (equivalently the maximum stack power).






Figure 1: Manufacturer polarisation curve (left) and resulting stack efficiency (right) used in the model.



As shown in Figure 1, the optimisation therefore captures the trade-off between operating fewer stacks at high current density or more stacks at lower current density.

title: Stack (PEM)
text:
Modularity
Commercial PEM electrolysers are typically manufactured as modular units with capacities of approximately 1 MW. Larger electrolysers are constructed by combining many identical modules.
The modular approach offers several practical advantages:

repeatable manufacturing
manageable electrical voltages and currents
improved thermal management
easier transport and installation
simplified maintenance and replacement

The model therefore represents an electrolyser as a collection of identical stack modules.

title: Stack (PEM)
text:
Module Switching
Because the electrolyser is modular, not every stack module has to operate simultaneously.
For every operating point, the model selects the number of active modules that maximises hydrogen output after the BOP and compression loads are supplied. Whenever all available power is used, this is the same as maximising system efficiency; the two differ only when surplus power is curtailed at the reference current density. The available electrical power is then distributed across the active modules.
This operational flexibility also alleviates the minimum-load limitation of PEM stacks, which is typically around 10% of the rated module capacity; the model uses 10% of the module rating (1000 kW).
For example, a 10 MW electrolyser consisting of ten 1 MW modules can operate at only one active module and 10% load. The minimum system load therefore becomes approximately 100 kW rather than 1 MW, allowing hydrogen production to continue during periods of low wind generation without operating individual stacks below their safe operating limit.
Module switching is assumed to occur without efficiency or lifetime penalties.

title: Stack (PEM)
text:
Stack Overplanting
The modular architecture naturally allows installation of more stack capacity than the maximum available electrical input. This is referred to here as stack overplanting.
Operating a larger installed stack capacity reduces the average current density of each active module. Lower current density increases conversion efficiency and slows stack degradation.
These benefits come at the expense of additional stack CAPEX. When overplanting cases are compared, the system scope greatly influences the outcome. As the scope expands, the optimum generally shifts towards larger stack capacities and higher efficiencies, as stack costs become a smaller fraction of the total system investment. See the box below for a worked example.






NoteExample: Why the optimisation scope matters



Consider first an electrolyser system consisting only of the power electronics, stacks and balance of plant.
If the stack represents roughly 30% of the total electrolyser cost, increasing the installed stack capacity by 50% increases the overall system CAPEX by approximately 15%. Such an investment is only justified when the resulting efficiency improvement produces comparable lifetime savings.
Now consider the complete offshore hydrogen production system, including wind turbines, electrical infrastructure, offshore installation and export systems.
Within this larger system the stack may represent only 5% of the total investment A 50% increase in installed stack capacity therefore increases total project cost by only around 2.5%, making relatively small efficiency improvements economically worthwhile.
This illustrates why component optimisation should always be performed within the context of the complete energy system rather than considering each component independently.

title: Stack (PEM)
text:
Degradation
Efficiency loss
PEM stacks gradually degrade during operation. As degradation progresses, the cell voltage increases, reducing the electrical efficiency of hydrogen production. The model assumes linear degradation with accumulated full-load operating hours with a fractional efficiency loss of 0.0018 per 1000 full-load hours.
Stack replacement
Eventually the efficiency loss becomes sufficiently large that replacing the stack is economically preferable to continued operation. In practice, approximately 10% performance degradation is commonly considered end-of-life; the model uses this threshold.
Ex-post energy penalty
Degradation is applied after the operating calculation, as an energy penalty. Operation, module selection and equipment sizing remain at beginning of life. Let \(r\) be the degradation rate per full-load hour, \(F\) the stacks’ annual full-load hours (annual stack energy divided by installed stack capacity), \(d_\mathrm{EOL}\) the end-of-life loss and \(N\) the project life in years. The loss grows by \(g=rF\) per year and resets at each replacement, after \(T=d_\mathrm{EOL}/g\) years. With \(k=\lfloor N/T\rfloor\) complete stack lives and remainder \(R=N-kT\), the project-average loss and the lifetime production factor are:
\[
\bar d=\frac{k\,d_\mathrm{EOL}T/2+gR^2/2}{N},
\qquad
f_\mathrm{life}=1-\bar d.
\]
Delivered hydrogen is multiplied by \(f_\mathrm{life}\) (implemented in lifetime_production_factor in model/hydrogen_production/stack.py). Degradation-driven increases in BOP load are not modelled. The replacement cost still uses the separate stack-replacement-life input, which should be set consistently with \(T\).
Effect of partial-load operation
Operating more installed stack capacity reduces the average current density of each module, slowing degradation and extending stack lifetime. This creates an additional economic incentive for stack overplanting, alongside the efficiency improvements described previously.






NoteExample: Stack overplanting and degradation



Assume a stack is replaced after reaching 10% degradation. With a fractional loss of 0.0018 per 1000 full-load hours, replacement occurs after approximately 55,600 full-load hours. Assuming an offshore wind capacity factor of 40%, this corresponds to roughly 15.9 calendar years. A 25-year project therefore requires at least one stack replacement. If this replacement is already unavoidable, installing additional stack capacity from the outset becomes an attractive alternative. The total stack material requirement over the project lifetime remains similar, while the system additionally benefits from:

Lower maintenance costs by avoiding mid-life replacement.
Higher efficiency through operation at lower current density.
Reduced degradation throughout the project lifetime.

This conclusion depends strongly on the assumption that degradation scales linearly with accumulated full-load hours.

title: Stack (PEM)
text:
Cost Model
Cost basis
The stack cost is based on the NREL bottom-up manufactured cost analysis for PEM water electrolyser stacks (Badgett et al. 2024). The NREL study evaluates a 1 MW PEM electrolyser stack and reports stack manufactured costs in 2020 US dollars per kW of stack capacity. The reported stack-only manufactured costs are:

316 $/kW at 10 MW/year manufacturing volume
183 $/kW at 100 MW/year manufacturing volume
164 $/kW at 1,000 MW/year manufacturing volume

These values exclude manufacturer markup, installation costs, soft costs and inflation. They are therefore used here as stack manufacturing cost inputs rather than complete installed electrolyser system costs.
The article reference case adopts 2 GW/year of stack manufacturing output as its supply-chain scenario, matching the approximate capacity of the reference wind farm. The farm’s one-time capacity does not itself imply this annual factory output; it is an explicit scenario assumption. NREL’s highest tabulated production rate is 1 GW/year, so the 2 GW/year stack cost below is an extrapolation. The 10 MW/year and 100 MW/year cases remain useful lower-volume sensitivities.
Reference-rated stack capacity
A complication is that the rated power of a PEM stack is not a purely physical property. For a given number of cells and active cell area, stack power depends on the current density at which the stack is rated. A higher rated current density gives more electrical power from the same physical stack and therefore reduces the apparent cost expressed in $/kW or €/MW, even if the stack itself has not become cheaper.
This is important because current density is treated explicitly in this model. Operating at higher current density increases the power output of a given stack, but it also increases cell voltage, reduces efficiency and accelerates degradation. Conversely, installing more stack capacity allows operation at lower current density, improving efficiency and lifetime at the expense of higher CAPEX.
The model therefore uses a reference-rated stack capacity as the cost-normalisation convention. This is the electrical capacity the installed stack would have if operated at a fixed reference current density of 3 A/cm2. The reference-rated capacity is used only for cost accounting; it does not imply that the stack must operate continuously at this current density.
NREL’s cost values are converted to this 3 A/cm² reference-rating convention where necessary. This avoids treating changes in rating current density as independent cost reductions. In the NREL cost-reduction waterfall, part of the reduction in $/kW arises from increased current density, because the same physical stack area is assigned a higher rated power. In this model, that mechanism is already captured explicitly through the polarisation curve: higher current density allows more power from the same installed stack, but with an efficiency and degradation penalty. Therefore, current-density-driven reductions in reported $/kW are not applied as a separate stack cost reduction.
Model implementation
The stack is modelled as a modular component whose cost scales linearly with installed reference-rated stack capacity. Linear scaling is used because larger PEM electrolyser systems are represented as multiple identical stack modules rather than as a single geometrically scaled stack. As a result, increasing installed stack capacity increases the number of modules, cells and active area approximately proportionally. No equipment-level scaling exponent is therefore applied to the stack itself.
Actual stack operation follows the module dispatch rule. At each time step, the model chooses the number of active modules and their operating current density. The corresponding electrical input, hydrogen production, efficiency and degradation are calculated from the polarisation curve. Reference-rated stack capacity is therefore a bookkeeping convention for cost only, while the physical and operational behaviour of the stack remains governed by current density.
Manufacturing-volume and purchase-cost calculation
NREL Table 10 isolates manufacturing-volume economies for the same reference design (Badgett et al. 2024). Raising annual output from 10 MW to 1 GW reduces manufactured stack cost from 316 to 164 USD/kW, a reduction of 152 USD/kW (48%). It does not include the additional technology changes in NREL’s Figure 27 waterfall, so the waterfall reductions are not added to the Table 10 result.
For the assumed 2 GW/year output, continue the logarithmic cost trend between NREL’s 100 MW/year and 1 GW/year points for another \(\log_{10}(2)\) decade. With \(M\) denoting annual manufacturing output [MW/year] and \(c_{\mathrm{mfg},2}\) the manufactured cost at NREL’s 2 A/cm² rating [USD/kW]:
\[
c_{\mathrm{mfg},2}(M)
=164-(183-164)\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{M}{1000\ \mathrm{MW/year}}\right),
\qquad M\geq1000\ \mathrm{MW/year}.
\]
At \(M=2000\) MW/year this gives approximately 158 USD/kW. This extension saves about 6 USD/kW beyond NREL’s 1 GW/year point. It is a local extrapolation, not a quoted NREL result or a forecast of further technology progress.
NREL rates its reference stack at \(j_2=2\) A/cm² and \(V_2=1.9\) V (Badgett et al. 2024). The model’s reference is \(j_3=3\) A/cm²; the supplied polarisation curve gives \(V_3\approx1.92\) V at that current density (Manufacturer G, n.d.). Holding cell count and active area fixed, rated power scales with \(jV\). The same physical stack therefore costs, per 3 A/cm²-rated kW:
\[
c_{\mathrm{mfg},3}
=c_{\mathrm{mfg},2}(2000)
\frac{j_2V_2}{j_3V_3}
\approx158\frac{2(1.9)}{3(1.92)}
\approx104\ \mathrm{USD}_{2020}/\mathrm{kW}.
\]
This is a rating-normalisation step, not a second manufacturing saving. Applying NREL’s 50% manufacturer markup, the U.S. CPI-U annual averages of 258.811 (2020) and 321.943 (2025), and the ECB 2025 average of 1.1300 USD/EUR gives:
\[
c_{\mathrm{stack,purchase},2025}
=c_{\mathrm{mfg},3}\,(1.5)
\frac{321.943}{258.811}\frac{1}{1.1300}
\approx172\ \mathrm{EUR}_{2025}/\mathrm{kW}.
\]
The rounded article reference is 175 EUR/kW of 3 A/cm² reference-rated stack capacity. It is an equipment-purchase estimate, not installed offshore cost. The fixed input stack-purchase-unit-cost remains unset in the executable model; this page records the adopted calculation basis pending implementation in the shared inputs and model.
Scope distinction
Only the stack cost is included in this component model. Balance-of-plant equipment, power electronics, installation, offshore structures and other system-level costs are represented elsewhere in the model. This distinction is important because the NREL report also provides full electrolyser system costs, but those include balance-of-plant components that are outside the scope of this stack page.
Stack replacement costs are calculated using the same specific stack cost assumption as the initial stack.

title: Stack (PEM)
text:
Availability
The modular architecture provides inherent redundancy because individual stack modules can be isolated without shutting down the complete electrolyser. A stack availability of 99.5% is assumed throughout this study.

title: Stack (PEM)

Installation and Mass
Stack installation is included within the installation model of the complete electrolyser facility or turbine-integrated hydrogen production system.
A dedicated stack mass model is not yet included. If future work identifies stack mass as a significant driver for tower sizing, platform design or installation costs, this section should be expanded accordingly.

title: Energy and Availability
text:
Legacy Availability Values
Earlier documentation listed flat values between 98% and 100%, including conflicting 98.5% and 99.5% electrolyser-related values. Their subsystem boundaries and evidence are not sufficient to select one as the adopted factor.
Those values are therefore not active architecture-ledger inputs. Component owners may retain them as clearly labelled legacy assumptions or sensitivities until they are evidenced and scoped. In particular, 100% pipeline availability is only a zero-outage scenario, not a reliability conclusion.

title: Modelling Workflow
text:
The model evaluates one complete user-supplied case deterministically. Alternative designs and sensitivities are separate input records. The model does not run an optimizer or choose a preferred case.
Input and output classes are defined on Inputs, Parameters and Outputs.
The executable draft is in model/, with calculation modules named after their owning pages. It currently implements the two hydrogen branches. Electricity export remains documented but is not yet an executable scenario branch. tools/run_model.py reads one article TOML scenario and writes an explicit local result folder. Article case templates and sensitivity execution live beside the article under research_articles/turbine_level_hydrogen/.
The draft retains turbine-level power until conversion and solves stack, BOP and compression demand against the available bus power in each operating state. Zero-hour design states can establish equipment duty without adding annual production. Availability and lifetime-production adjustments follow the operating calculation. The current cost scope excludes development, shared owner engineering, insurance and owner contingency; included platform, installation and replacement gaps still prevent a complete LCOH.
The model README documents input tables, module boundaries and remaining interfaces. Missing scalar values stay blank in the central CSV and are reported as required inputs. Website rendering only builds shared display values and figures; it does not execute article cases.

title: Modelling Workflow
text:
Canonical Scalar Inputs
Adopted scalar inputs are stored once in model_data/inputs.csv, using stable, human-readable IDs. Website pages reference those IDs, and calculation and figure code reads the same numeric records. Explanations, evidence assessment, scope and limitations remain on the owning website page.
The website build validates IDs, values, units, classifications, price years and citation keys before rendering. It then calculates derived values and currency-only conversions. Generated display variables are not model inputs and must not be edited directly.

title: Modelling Workflow
text:
Execution Order

1. Validate the Case Record
Check that every required user input and fixed parameter:

has a value and unit;
belongs to one controlled class;
is applicable to the selected architecture;
lies within an adopted method or product envelope; and
does not conflict with another representation of the same quantity.

A missing required input returns not parameterized. A supplied value that violates a physical or technical constraint returns infeasible.


2. Select the Architecture Branch
Select exactly one of:

electricity export;
centralised offshore hydrogen production; or
decentralised turbine-integrated hydrogen production.

The architecture mapping determines which component owners are active. An excluded component contributes neither cost nor loss.


3. Calculate Resource, Layout and Gross Production
The wind and layout pages return:

the accepted turbine definition;
turbine coordinates and farm area;
gross and wake-adjusted production on the documented time basis; and
layout feasibility and rejection reasons.

Where time-varying wind data are used, the owning page retains its documented time step \(\Delta t\).


4. Construct Physical Inventories
Calculate, before cost:

turbine and foundation records;
cable or pipeline route sections and physical lengths;
platforms and equipment inventories;
equipment counts; and
installation-relevant masses, dimensions, lifts and loads.

Every downstream cost must consume an explicit physical quantity or a clearly labelled top-down factor.


5. Size or Select Discrete Equipment
Apply the deterministic rules owned by each component page, including ceiling or class-selection steps. The user supplies any design choice that is not uniquely determined by the documented rules.
A failed capacity, product-class, lift, route or operating-envelope check returns infeasible. An unresolved product set or sizing input returns not parameterized.


6. Calculate Energy in Physical Order
Starting from wake-adjusted turbine production:

apply component efficiency or conversion equations;
subtract auxiliary demand at its owning subsystem;
apply curtailment only where a documented capacity limit requires it;
calculate hydrogen mass where applicable; and
aggregate pre-availability annual energy.

Time-varying nonlinear performance may retain the component time step. Availability is not applied here unless the same effect is already embedded in the energy record.


7. Apply Annual Availability Once
Pass pre-availability annual energy to the architecture ledger on Energy and Availability.
Multiply only non-overlapping subsystem factors. A factor already embedded in the upstream energy record is not applied again. Parallel-unit and redundancy effects must already be combined by the component owner.


8. Aggregate Cost
Combine non-overlapping:

component supply CAPEX;
installation CAPEX;
shared project-cost fields;
required replacements;
decommissioning; and
annual OPEX.

Unknown required terms return not parameterized; they are not treated as zero.


9. Annualize and Report
Apply the common CRF method from Financial and Price-Basis Assumptions, then return the endpoint and units defined on System Boundary and Carrier-Cost Metrics.

Methodology
text:

Read the shared method in dependency order:

title: Cable and Pipeline Installation
text:
WarningIncomplete cost result



This page does not currently produce a complete cable- or TCP-installation CAPEX result. Cable lay tasks can be parameterized from ORBIT screening inputs, but burial-spread rates, survey productivity and rates, demobilisation, weather delay and exceptional scope remain unresolved. TCP additionally lacks a qualified product, vessel configuration, task times and matching spread rates.
A user-provided Van Oord cable-installation benchmark is materially higher than the earlier proxy calculation, but its contract boundary and price basis have not been independently evidenced in this repository. It remains a reconciliation item rather than a model input. Missing terms below return not parameterized, not zero.

title: Cable and Pipeline Installation
text:
1. How an Installation Campaign Works
Offshore installation converts supplied cable or pipe into a connected, protected and tested offshore asset. A typical cable campaign proceeds as follows:
mobilise the installation spread → load product at port → transit to site → survey or prepare the route → pull in the first end → lay the product → return to port and splice when required → pull in the second end → bury the route → inspect and survey the installation → test and complete the asset → demobilise
The activities are not always strictly sequential. Pull-ins occur around individual lay sections, not only after the complete route has been laid. An export-cable splice can interrupt laying when another product length is loaded. Burial and post-burial survey normally follow as separate campaigns in the reference method.
This page uses one time-and-rate framework for four installation subclasses:

66–132 kV inter-array cables;
320–525 kV HVDC export systems;
spoolable thermoplastic-composite-pipe (TCP) hydrogen infield pipelines; and
spoolable TCP hydrogen export pipelines.

The accounting framework is shared. Product configuration, task times, installation rates and feasibility limits remain subclass-specific.
Cost boundary
The installation boundary begins when the contracted spreads mobilise and ends after the offshore testing included in their installation scope.







Scope
Treatment




Cable or pipe manufacture and supply accessories
Excluded; owned by the relevant cable or pipeline page


Lay-spread mobilisation, loading, transit, laying, pull-ins, offshore splices, lay-spread testing and demobilisation
Included through lay-spread time


Burial-spread mobilisation, transit, trenching or burial, positioning and demobilisation
Included through burial-spread time


Independent ROV and survey campaigns or support
Included through ROV/survey-spread time


Crew, fuel, routine workboats and tugs, and contractor overhead
Included in the applicable spread day rate


Crossings, landfall, protection materials and exceptional civil work
Added separately when outside the spread scope


Converter stations, substations, hydrogen compression, development, finance, contingency, OPEX and decommissioning
Excluded; owned elsewhere in the model



Every vessel, activity and material is charged once. If an ROV is onboard the lay vessel and included in the lay rate, it is not also assigned a separate ROV spread. If burial is performed by an integrated lay-and-bury spread, the separate burial term is zero and an integrated rate replaces the reference split.

title: Cable and Pipeline Installation
text:
2. Three-Spread Installation Cost Model
The reference calculation separates installation into laying, burial and ROV/survey spreads. Each spread produces an explicit number of chargeable days, which is later multiplied by its matching all-in day rate.









Spread
Time output
Rate input
Cost contribution




Laying
\(T_{\mathrm{lay}}\)
\(r_{\mathrm{lay}}\)
Lay-spread days multiplied by lay-spread rate


Burial

Burial-spread days multiplied by burial-spread rate


ROV/survey
\(T_{\mathrm{ROV}}\)

The three times are spread-days, not sequential project days. A lay vessel and an ROV/survey vessel working on the same calendar day each incur one chargeable day. Their costs therefore add even though their activities are concurrent.
For cable subclasses, ORBIT is the preferred source of task durations. The equations on this page define the required ORBIT configuration, map its task outputs to the three spreads and provide a transparent fallback when only the published task inputs are available. The same task is not estimated independently in ORBIT and again on this page.
Day-rate boundary








Rate

\(r_{\mathrm{ROV}}\)
