Specialist investigation or exceptional intervention packages



Mobilisation and demobilisation are represented as chargeable spread days. A quotation that prices them as lump sums must first be converted into an equivalent time-and-rate treatment or recorded as a separate fixed cost with a clearly non-overlapping boundary.
The model assumes full day-rate charging during weather standby. If a contract uses reduced standby rates, the weather-cost treatment must be changed rather than represented only by a time uplift.
ORBIT cable reference set

They are screening inputs rather than observed project performance. For cable-lay screening only, this page treats the normalized cable-vessel proxy as a complete lay-spread rate including crew, fuel, routine workboats and tugs, and contractor overhead. It must be replaced together with its stated boundary for a commercial estimate. The same rate is not assigned to burial. ORBIT does not assign its generic support vessel to a cable-survey campaign, so that vessel’s rate is retained as source context but is not used in the installation calculation.
ORBIT’s published methodology tables show 1.0 km/h for separate laying and 0.5 km/h for separate burial, while the reviewed version 1.3 executable defaults are 0.4 km/h for both (National Laboratory of the Rockies, n.d.). The cable-lay screening calculation uses the executable lay value so that it can be reproduced from the pinned code revision. The burial value is retained as source context but is not adopted without a route soil, burial tool and matching spread.

title: Cable and Pipeline Installation
text:
3. Physical Quantities and Installation Configuration
ORBIT can estimate installation time only after the physical system and installation method have been configured correctly. Three length measures remain distinct.








Quantity
Definition
Model use




Route-kilometre
Horizontal centreline distance between route endpoints
Defines the corridor


Physical cable- or pipeline-kilometre
Total product installed across every distinct asset
Controls product mass, loading and supplied length


Pass-kilometre
Distance travelled while one physical cable or pipeline is installed
Controls lay and burial time; survey passes are counted separately



For asset type \(a\), physical length is:
\[
L_{\mathrm{physical},a}
=
N_{\mathrm{parallel},a}L_{\mathrm{route},a}(1+s_a)
+L_{\mathrm{vert},a}.
\]








Symbol
Definition
Unit




\(N_{\mathrm{parallel},a}\)
Number of distinct physical cables or pipes
count


\(L_{\mathrm{route},a}\)
Horizontal route length
route-km


\(s_a\)
Installation slack fraction
dimensionless


\(L_{\mathrm{vert},a}\)
Total separately calculated vertical and structure allowance
km


\(L_{\mathrm{physical},a}\)
Total installed product length
physical km



Slack is not added when project section lengths already include it.
ORBIT installs every array-cable section and export cable individually. The reference model therefore permits only one physical cable or pipeline in each lay or burial pass. For spread type \(x\):
\[
N_{\mathrm{pass},x,a}
=
N_{\mathrm{parallel},a},
\qquad
L_{\mathrm{pass},x,a}
=
N_{\mathrm{pass},x,a}L_{\mathrm{route},a}.
\]
For non-identical sections or routes, actual traversed lengths are summed:
\[
L_{\mathrm{pass},x}
=
\sum_m L_m.
\]
Here \(x\) identifies the lay or burial spread, \(N_{\mathrm{pass},x,a}\) is its pass count and \(L_{\mathrm{pass},x,a}\) is pass-km. Survey length is calculated from its own required route passes because a survey can cover a corridor rather than every individual product.
TenneT calls its 2 GW export connection one cable system, but defines that system as four individual cables: positive pole, negative pole, metallic return and fibre-optic cable (TenneT, n.d.). Under the one-cable-per-pass ORBIT convention, one TenneT reference system therefore contains four physical lay units and four lay passes. Product length, mass and loading are calculated separately for each cable type; the indicative power-cable mass is not applied to the metallic return or fibre cable. This is a transparent screening convention, not evidence that TenneT’s contractor necessarily installs the four-cable bundle in four separate operations.
Lay-vessel feasibility and selection
Product linear mass affects two separate installation decisions. First, it determines how much product a given vessel can carry. Second, together with reel and handling requirements, it determines which vessel classes can perform the work. The second effect is material for TCP: a light spoolable pipeline can make a smaller multipurpose lay spread feasible, while a heavy cable may require a larger cable-lay vessel.
For candidate lay spread \(v\) and lay unit \(m\), the candidate-specific product length per load is:
\[
L_{\mathrm{load},m,v}
=
\min\left(
\frac{M_{\mathrm{usable},v}}{\lambda_{\mathrm{product},m}},
L_{\mathrm{reel/partition},m,v},
L_{\mathrm{manufacturing},m},
L_{\mathrm{handling},m,v}
\right).
\]
A vessel is not qualified from payload alone. The product supplier and installation contractor must also verify minimum bend radius, tension, overboarding, dynamic loads, station keeping, water depth and route-specific operating limits. Those checks are retained at the highest defensible level as a qualification gate rather than reproduced through an unevidenced installation-engineering model:
\[
I_{\mathrm{qualified},m,v}
=
\begin{cases}
1, & \text{all product-, vessel- and route-specific checks pass},\\
0, & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]
The feasible candidate set is therefore:
\[
\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{feasible},m}
=
\left\{
v\;\middle|\;
L_{\mathrm{load},m,v}\ge L_{\mathrm{minimum},m}
\quad\text{and}\quad
I_{\mathrm{qualified},m,v}=1
\right\}.
\]
The campaign-feasible set is \(\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{feasible}}=\bigcap_m\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{feasible},m}\) because the selected spread must qualify for every lay unit assigned to it.








Symbol
Definition
Unit




\(v\)
Candidate lay spread or vessel class
–


\(M_{\mathrm{usable},v}\)
Usable product payload of candidate \(v\) after reel and deck equipment
t


\(\lambda_{\mathrm{product},m}\)
Linear mass of the selected product for lay unit \(m\)
t/physical km


\(L_{\mathrm{reel/partition},m,v}\)
Product length permitted by the candidate storage arrangement
physical km/load


\(L_{\mathrm{manufacturing},m}\)
Available continuous manufactured product length
physical km/load


\(L_{\mathrm{handling},m,v}\)
Product length permitted by the qualified handling and installation arrangement
physical km/load


\(L_{\mathrm{minimum},m}\)
Minimum continuous product length that must be carried between permitted field connections for lay unit \(m\)
km


\(I_{\mathrm{qualified},m,v}\)
Supplier- and contractor-confirmed installation qualification gate
binary


\(\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{feasible},m}\)
Candidate spreads that satisfy the explicit loading constraint and qualification gate
set



Loading, reloads, transit, production, interface tasks and weather are then calculated separately for every feasible candidate, because vessel capacity and operating limits can change both time and cost. The cost-minimising qualified lay spread is:
\[
v^*
=
\underset{v\in\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{feasible}}}{\arg\min}
\left[
r_{\mathrm{lay},v}T_{\mathrm{lay},v}
+C_{\mathrm{lay,fixed},v}
\right].
\]
Here \(r_{\mathrm{lay},v}\) is the all-in day rate for candidate \(v\), \(T_{\mathrm{lay},v}\) is its chargeable campaign time and \(C_{\mathrm{lay,fixed},v}\) contains only explicitly quoted lay-spread costs not already represented by time and rate. Lower product mass can admit smaller candidates with lower rates, but the selected spread still depends on load count, productivity, mobilisation, operability and commercial boundary. If candidate-specific TCP rates are unavailable, the model reports the feasible vessel classes as alternative outcomes; it does not select \(v^*\) or calculate TCP installation CAPEX.

title: Cable and Pipeline Installation
text:
4. Lay-Spread Time
The lay-spread calculation follows ORBIT’s cable-installation task logic. ORBIT explicitly represents mobilisation, product loading, vessel storage, port returns, route laying, positioning, pull-ins, offshore splicing, termination/testing and transit (National Laboratory of the Rockies, n.d.). Demobilisation remains a separate unresolved input because the reviewed cable module does not contain a general demobilisation task.
Chargeable lay time is divided into port or other non-weather-uplifted time and offshore weather-exposed time:
\[
T_{\mathrm{lay,base}}
=
T_{\mathrm{lay,nonweather}}
+T_{\mathrm{lay,offshore,base}}.
\]








Symbol
Definition
Unit




\(T_{\mathrm{lay,base}}\)
Lay time before weather uplift
day


\(T_{\mathrm{lay,nonweather}}\)
Port and other defined lay time not exposed to the offshore weather uplift
day


\(T_{\mathrm{lay,offshore,base}}\)
Offshore-exposed lay time before weather uplift
day



Weather is applied later, after all base tasks have been counted.
Product per load
For a selected vessel \(v^*\), \(L_{\mathrm{load},m}=L_{\mathrm{load},m,v^*}\) from the candidate calculation in Section 3. Before selection, load counts and campaign time are evaluated separately for every feasible candidate. This preserves the discrete trade-off between a smaller vessel with more loads and a larger vessel with a higher day rate.








Symbol
Definition
Unit




\(L_{\mathrm{load},m}\)
Effective product length per load for lay unit \(m\) and the selected vessel
physical km/load


\(L_{\mathrm{physical},m}\)
Physical product length of lay unit \(m\)
physical km


\(L_{m,g}\)
Length of product \(m\) assigned to vessel load \(g\)
physical km


\(N_{\mathrm{load},c}\)
Port loads assigned to separately mobilised lay campaign \(c\)
count


\(N_{\mathrm{load}}\), \(N_{\mathrm{reload}}\)
Total port loads and subsequent reloads
count



One vessel load can contain several complete array-cable sections or other compatible products. A valid loading plan assigns product to loads subject to:
\[
\sum_m \lambda_{\mathrm{product},m}L_{m,g}
\le M_{\mathrm{usable},v},
\qquad
0\le L_{m,g}\le L_{\mathrm{load},m,v}.
\]
Every physical section must remain complete unless the product and installation plan permit a field connection. Reel partitions, storage compatibility and installation order must therefore be checked in addition to total mass. This is a discrete packing problem; dividing total campaign mass by vessel payload gives only a lower bound when the detailed loading plan is unavailable.
The ORBIT reference carousel has a 13,000 t maximum mass. It defines one cable-vessel candidate rather than a universal installation capacity. For example, an indicative 65 t/km HVDC pole cable would be mass-limited to 200 physical km/load before reel, manufacturing and handling limits are applied. That result is not transferred to the metallic-return or fibre-optic cables.
Loads and reloads are counted by separately mobilised lay campaign \(c\):
\[
N_{\mathrm{load}}=\sum_c N_{\mathrm{load},c},
\qquad
N_{\mathrm{reload}}
=
\sum_c\max(0,N_{\mathrm{load},c}-1).
\]
Port loading time is the sum of the actual load operations:
\[
T_{\mathrm{port\ load}}
=
\sum_g t_{\mathrm{load},g}.
\]
ORBIT uses six hours for both the initial load and each reload (National Laboratory of the Rockies, n.d.). This is product-loading time only. It does not include the return transit and repositioning needed for a reload.
Pass count and load count are independent. Four physical export-cable passes do not by themselves prove four port loads: the result depends on the qualified storage and loading plan. Conversely, one continuous cable can require several loads and offshore splices.
Port returns
For one-way distance \(D_{\mathrm{port}}\) between the work site and loading port, vessel transit speed \(v_{\mathrm{transit}}\) in km/h and repositioning time \(t_{\mathrm{reposition}}\) in days:
\[
T_{\mathrm{port\ return}}
=
\sum_c \max(0,N_{\mathrm{load},c}-1)
\left(
\frac{2D_{\mathrm{port}}}{24v_{\mathrm{transit}}}
+t_{\mathrm{reposition}}
\right).
\]
The port loading itself remains in \(T_{\mathrm{port\ load}}\), so it is not included again in this expression.
The ORBIT reference cable vessel uses \(v_{\mathrm{transit}}=11.5\) km/h. Its reload sequence includes the outbound and return transits; onsite positioning associated with an offshore splice is counted in the splice task below and is not added as \(t_{\mathrm{reposition}}\).
Route laying
Lay production time is lay pass-km divided by the selected operating lay rate, summed over passes \(p\):
\[
T_{\mathrm{route\ lay}}
=
\sum_p
\frac{L_{\mathrm{pass,lay},p}}{q_{\mathrm{lay},p}}.
\]
The reviewed ORBIT version 1.3 implementation uses \(q_{\mathrm{lay}}=0.4\) km/h, equivalent to 9.6 km/day of continuous operation (National Laboratory of the Rockies, n.d.). This is an operating rate, not an achieved weather-inclusive campaign rate. Product handling, stops, interfaces and weather are represented separately.
Pull-ins, splicing and testing
The model preserves the number of physical interfaces and splices because they create material step changes in vessel time. It does not require every minor handling action as a separate model input. Instead, a sourced aggregate duration is assigned to each event type \(e\):
\[
T_{\mathrm{event}}
=
\sum_e\frac{N_e t_e}{24}.
\]









Event type \(e\)
Aggregate duration \(t_e\)
Included ORBIT tasks
Counting rule




Array-cable section
27 h/section
Positioning, preparation, two pull-ins, two termination/test tasks and lowering
Once per physical array-cable section


Export power-cable interface sequence
26 h/cable
Landfall and offshore-end positioning, preparation, pull-in, termination/test and lowering
Once per qualifying export power cable; metallic-return and fibre tasks require matching inputs


Offshore splice
51.5 h/splice
Positioning, cable recovery, splicing and lowering
Once per required continuous-route load break



The aggregate durations are derived from the executable ORBIT defaults listed in Section 2 (National Laboratory of the Rockies, n.d.). They apply only while the lay spread remains occupied. Retaining the underlying task values in the source-input table preserves traceability, while the calculation uses the event totals that materially determine campaign duration.
For array cables, a reload normally supplies additional discrete cable sections and does not automatically create an offshore splice. For a continuous export route, exceeding the available continuous product length can require both a reload and an inline splice.
Lay-time aggregation
Non-weather-uplifted lay time is:
\[
T_{\mathrm{lay,nonweather}}
=
T_{\mathrm{mob,lay}}
+T_{\mathrm{port\ load}}
+T_{\mathrm{demob,lay}}.
\]
Base offshore-exposed lay time is:
\[
\begin{aligned}
T_{\mathrm{lay,offshore,base}}
={}&
T_{\mathrm{site\ transit}}
+T_{\mathrm{route\ lay}}
+T_{\mathrm{port\ return}}\\
&+T_{\mathrm{event}}
\end{aligned}
\]
All terms in the two aggregation equations are chargeable days. \(T_{\mathrm{mob,lay}}\) is 1.5 full-rate-equivalent days in the cable screening case, representing ORBIT’s three calendar days at 50% of the day rate. \(T_{\mathrm{demob,lay}}\) remains unresolved. \(T_{\mathrm{site\ transit}}\) is initial offshore transit. Every event is assigned once.

title: Cable and Pipeline Installation
text:
5. Burial-Spread Time
The reference method uses a separate burial spread. Its task sequence is mobilisation, transit, tool deployment and setup, burial or pre-trenching passes, repositioning, tool recovery and demobilisation.
Non-weather-uplifted burial time is mobilisation and demobilisation:
\[
T_{\mathrm{bury,nonweather}}
=
T_{\mathrm{mob,bury}}
+T_{\mathrm{demob,bury}}.
\]
Base offshore-exposed burial time is:
\[
\begin{aligned}
T_{\mathrm{bury,offshore,base}}
={}&
T_{\mathrm{transit,bury}}
+T_{\mathrm{setup,bury}}\\
&+\sum_p
\frac{L_{\mathrm{pass,bury},p}}{q_{\mathrm{bury},p}}
+T_{\mathrm{reposition,bury}}\\
&+T_{\mathrm{recovery,bury}}.
\end{aligned}
\]

T_{\mathrm{bury,base}}
=
T_{\mathrm{bury,nonweather}}
+T_{\mathrm{bury,offshore,base}}.
\]

These are reference defaults, not adopted base-case inputs. Route-specific soil, burial depth, tool selection, mobilisation, transit, deployment, recovery, demobilisation and the matching spread rate are required before burial time and cost are parameterized.
Burial pass length is not assumed equal to lay pass length. Sections near structures, landfall or designed protection zones may have different burial lengths, but only one physical cable or pipeline is buried in each modeled pass.
Rock, mattresses and crossing structures are excluded from burial-spread time unless the selected burial rate explicitly includes the corresponding installation method and materials. Their material and specialist-package costs normally remain exceptional.
If laying and burial are physically integrated, this separate calculation is not used. The project instead requires one integrated duration and one integrated spread rate.

title: Cable and Pipeline Installation
text:
6. ROV and Survey-Spread Time
The ROV/survey spread can perform independent pre-lay, as-laid, post-burial or inspection campaigns and can support laying, burial or interfaces. Independent survey time is calculated from surveyed pass length and survey rate:
\[
T_{\mathrm{survey,independent,base}}
=
\sum_k
\frac{L_{\mathrm{survey},k}}{q_{\mathrm{survey},k}}
+T_{\mathrm{ROV,interface}}.
\]








Symbol
Definition
Unit




\(T_{\mathrm{survey,independent,base}}\)
Independent survey and interface time before weather uplift
day


\(L_{\mathrm{survey},k}\)
Route or pass length surveyed in activity \(k\)
km


\(q_{\mathrm{survey},k}\)
Operating survey rate for activity \(k\)
km/day


\(T_{\mathrm{ROV,interface}}\)
Independent ROV time at pull-ins, joints, crossings or other interfaces
day



ORBIT’s cable module supplies no independent survey-pass count or survey production rate. Its generic support-vessel transit speed is not a proxy for survey productivity. Survey scope, achieved production, mobilisation and the matching complete-spread rate therefore remain site-specific or contractor inputs; until they are provided, \(T_{\mathrm{ROV}}\) and the ROV/survey cost term are not parameterized.
ROV support that accompanies another spread is based on that spread’s actual weather-adjusted offshore time:
\[
T_{\mathrm{ROV,support}}
=
\alpha_{\mathrm{lay}}T_{\mathrm{lay,offshore}}
+\alpha_{\mathrm{bury}}T_{\mathrm{bury,offshore}},
\]
where \(\alpha_{\mathrm{lay}}\) and \(\alpha_{\mathrm{bury}}\) are the fractions of lay- and burial-spread offshore time requiring a separately charged ROV/survey spread. They lie between 0 and 1 and must be defined from the installation method.
The reference lay and burial campaigns do not overlap. If support windows do overlap, \(T_{\mathrm{ROV,support}}\) is the duration of their union rather than the arithmetic sum of overlapping days.
Total ROV/survey-spread time is:
\[
T_{\mathrm{ROV}}
=
T_{\mathrm{mob,ROV}}
+T_{\mathrm{demob,ROV}}
+T_{\mathrm{survey,independent}}
+T_{\mathrm{ROV,support}}.
\]
Here \(T_{\mathrm{survey,independent}}\) is weather-adjusted independent survey time, \(T_{\mathrm{ROV,support}}\) is concurrent support time, and \(T_{\mathrm{ROV}}\) is total chargeable ROV/survey spread-days. Mobilisation and demobilisation are inputs for the selected survey spread; ORBIT’s generic support-vessel mobilisation is not adopted without a demonstrated survey scope.
Concurrent support is a separate spread cost, not additional project elapsed time. If ROV and survey equipment are onboard and included in the lay or burial day rate, the corresponding \(\alpha\) is zero and those days are not charged again.

title: Cable and Pipeline Installation
text:
7. Weather and Total Installation CAPEX
Weather is represented by a transparent time uplift rather than an ORBIT discrete-event weather simulation. Port loading and other defined non-weather tasks are not uplifted.
The ORBIT duration used here must therefore exclude simulated weather delay. If a weather-inclusive ORBIT result is used instead, the corresponding uplift \(w\) is set to zero.
For laying:
\[
T_{\mathrm{lay}}
=
T_{\mathrm{lay,nonweather}}
+(1+w_{\mathrm{lay}})
T_{\mathrm{lay,offshore,base}}.
\]
The weather-adjusted lay offshore time used by ROV support is:
\[
T_{\mathrm{lay,offshore}}
=
(1+w_{\mathrm{lay}})
T_{\mathrm{lay,offshore,base}}.
\]
For burial, the model separates any fixed non-weather time from offshore-exposed work:
\[
T_{\mathrm{bury}}
=
T_{\mathrm{bury,nonweather}}
+(1+w_{\mathrm{bury}})
T_{\mathrm{bury,offshore,base}}.
\]
The weather-adjusted burial offshore time used by ROV support is:
\[
T_{\mathrm{bury,offshore}}
=
(1+w_{\mathrm{bury}})
T_{\mathrm{bury,offshore,base}}.
\]
For independent survey:
\[
T_{\mathrm{survey,independent}}
=
(1+w_{\mathrm{ROV}})
T_{\mathrm{survey,independent,base}}.
\]

Definition
Unit

No numerical weather uplift is adopted until an evidence basis is provided. Different spreads require different weather treatment because their operating limits differ. If weather evidence is unavailable, base exposed time can be reported, but weather-adjusted duration and installation CAPEX remain not parameterized.
Once the three chargeable spread times are known, installation CAPEX is:
\[
C_{\mathrm{installation}}
=
r_{\mathrm{lay}}T_{\mathrm{lay}}

+C_{\mathrm{exceptional}}.

For a campaign selected from candidate spreads, \(r_{\mathrm{lay}}=r_{\mathrm{lay},v^*}\) and \(T_{\mathrm{lay}}=T_{\mathrm{lay},v^*}\). A missing candidate-specific TCP rate therefore blocks the numerical TCP lay-cost term; it is not replaced by the cable-vessel rate or set to zero.
Exceptional cost is:
\[
C_{\mathrm{exceptional}}
=
N_{\mathrm{cross}}C_{\mathrm{cross}}
+L_{\mathrm{protection}}c_{\mathrm{protection}}
+N_{\mathrm{landfall}}C_{\mathrm{landfall}}
+C_{\mathrm{other}}.
\]
Here \(N_{\mathrm{cross}}\) and \(N_{\mathrm{landfall}}\) are counts; \(C_{\mathrm{cross}}\) and \(C_{\mathrm{landfall}}\) are EUR2025 per item; \(L_{\mathrm{protection}}\) is protected route length in km; \(c_{\mathrm{protection}}\) is EUR2025/km; and \(C_{\mathrm{other}}\) is any other explicitly scoped exceptional cost in EUR2025.
Crossings, landfall, protection materials and exceptional civil work remain site-specific. A term is set to zero only when the matching spread quotation explicitly includes the same scope.
Constant-EUR2025 normalisation
Each spread rate and exceptional cost is escalated in its original currency before conversion to euros:
\[
C_{2025,\mathrm{EUR}}
=
C_{y,s}
\frac{I_{s,k}(2025)}{I_{s,k}(y)}
FX_{\mathrm{EUR}/s}(2025)
G_{\mathrm{market}}.
\]



Symbol
Definition




\(C_{y,s}\)
Source cost in currency \(s\) and price year \(y\)


\(I_{s,k}\)
Selected index for cost type \(k\) in the source market


\(FX_{\mathrm{EUR}/s}\)
Euros per unit of source currency


\(G_{\mathrm{market}}\)
Separately stated geographic-market factor



ORBIT version 1.3 states its vessel-library costs in 2024 USD (National Laboratory of the Rockies, n.d.). The screening conversion uses annual-average U.S. CPI-U values of 313.689 for 2024 and 321.943 for 2025, followed by the ECB 2025 annual-average exchange rate of USD 1.1300 per EUR (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics 2026b, 2026a; European Central Bank 2026):
\[
F
=
\frac{321.943}{313.689}\frac{1}{1.1300}
=
0.9082413\ \mathrm{EUR}_{2025}/\mathrm{USD}_{2024}.
\]
The factor gives 219,041 EUR2025/day for ORBIT’s 241,171 USD/day cable vessel and 111,440 EUR2025/day for its 122,699 USD/day generic support vessel. The first value is adopted only as a provisional complete cable-lay-spread rate under the explicit inclusion boundary in Section 2. The burial and ROV/survey rates remain unresolved because ORBIT does not demonstrate that either vessel proxy represents those complete scopes.

title: Cable and Pipeline Installation
text:
8. Installation-Subclass Differences
The ORBIT task structure is directly applicable only to cable installation. The shared equations can describe TCP work, but cable operating rates and task times are not transferred to TCP.









Subclass
Lay configuration
Loading, pull-in and splice treatment
Burial and ROV treatment




66–132 kV inter-array cable
One static three-core section per lay pass
Vessel loads multiple discrete sections; two pull-ins per section; a reload does not normally create an inline splice
Burial pass count follows individual cable routes; survey and ROV scope follows the selected cable method


320–525 kV HVDC export
One physical cable per pass. The TenneT 2 GW reference has four physical cables and therefore four modeled lay passes (TenneT, n.d.)
Product-specific capacity controls reloads; continuous-route load breaks may create inline splices; pull-ins occur at landfall and offshore interfaces
Each physical cable is buried separately in the screening model; landfall and protection remain separate


Spoolable TCP hydrogen infield
One qualified TCP length per lay pass
Reel exchange, J-tube pull-through, field end fitting, tie-in and testing require TCP-specific inputs
Burial, stability and ROV requirements depend on qualified product and route design


Spoolable TCP hydrogen export
Same physical accounting, subject to long-route feasibility
Repeated reels and intermediate connectors can dominate time; no cable splice or pull-in defaults are used
All production, burial, survey and support inputs require supplier and contractor evidence



Public 66 kV examples span approximately 20–50 t/km, so loading must use the selected cable rather than voltage alone (Thor Offshore Wind Farm Environmental Material, n.d.).
An indicative 2,500 mm² copper 525 kV submarine cable has a linear mass of approximately 65 t/km, but this is not a universal HVDC mass assumption and applies neither to TenneT’s metallic return nor to its fibre-optic cable (Prysmian Group, n.d.; TenneT, n.d.).
Manufacturer information supports horizontal TCP lay from a small multipurpose vessel and continuous lengths of approximately 3–6 km, depending on diameter and pressure (Strohm, n.d.-b). This is the physical basis for admitting a smaller candidate spread to the vessel-selection calculation. The installation-cost benefit does not come from product mass directly: it arises when the lighter product and its handling envelope make that smaller spread feasible and the matching all-in rate is lower than the rate for the qualifying cable-lay spread. These are generic product-family capabilities, not a qualified hydrogen design point. DNV-ST-F119 supplies the offshore TCP standard basis, while DNV’s hydrogen work identifies hydrogen-specific qualification gaps (DNV-ST-F119 2019; DNV, n.d.).
Until product and contractor qualification is available, the model reports two vessel-class outcomes rather than forcing one selection:








TCP outcome
Qualification result
Cost treatment




Small multipurpose-vessel subclass
Payload and reel constraints pass and \(I_{\mathrm{qualified},m,v}=1\) for the small spread
Use the matching small-spread task inputs and day rate when supplied; currently not parameterized


Specialist lay-vessel subclass
The small spread fails payload, reel or qualification requirements
Evaluate the next qualified vessel class with its own inputs and rate; currently not parameterized



An offshore TCP export calculation requires:

a named hydrogen-qualified product and operating envelope;
route-specific pressure, stability and installation design;
continuous-length, reel and field-connection information;
a qualified vessel and overboarding configuration;
bend, tension, collapse and pull-through verification;
laying, burial and survey production rates;
interface and connector task times; and
all-in lay, burial and ROV/survey day rates.

An 80–100 km export route is far longer than the public 3–6 km continuous-length range. Until these inputs are available, TCP installation remains not parameterized. ORBIT cable rates, steel-pipeline rates and conventional flexible-pipeline rates are not substituted.

Required assertions

Physical product length increases with every parallel asset.
Every modeled lay and burial pass contains exactly one physical cable or pipeline.
A lay spread is considered only after the explicit loading constraints pass and the supplier/contractor qualification gate equals one.
Product linear mass changes candidate-specific product per load and can change the feasible vessel set; it does not directly impose a day rate.
Each feasible candidate’s campaign time is calculated using that candidate’s capacity, task inputs and operating limits before spread selection.
One TenneT 2 GW reference system produces four physical cable passes; the system count is not substituted for the cable count.
Every load satisfies product-specific mass, storage, partition and handling limits; a total-mass ceiling is not treated as a proven packing plan.
The initial product load is counted once per separately mobilised lay campaign and every later load in that campaign creates one reload.
An array-cable reload does not automatically create an inline splice.
A continuous export-cable load break creates a splice only when required by the product and installation plan.
Port loading is not weather-uplifted.
Weather is applied once to each exposed spread time.
Concurrent ROV support is charged as ROV spread-days without extending project elapsed time.
Overlapping ROV support windows are counted once for the ROV spread.
ROV or survey equipment included in another spread rate is not charged separately.
Crew, fuel, routine workboats and tugs, and contractor overhead are not added outside the spread rates.
Exceptional scope included in a spread quotation is not added again.
Any missing material task time, qualification, weather input or matching spread rate returns not parameterized, not zero.

Current limitations







Limitation
Consequence




ORBIT values are task and example-vessel defaults rather than achieved project performance
Cable-time and spread-cost results remain screening estimates


ORBIT documentation and version 1.3 code disagree on lay and burial speeds
The pinned executable defaults are used and the discrepancy is disclosed


ORBIT installs individual cables and does not demonstrate TenneT’s actual bundled-installation method
Four separate passes are a screening convention that may overstate HVDC time


No project weather input is available
Weather-adjusted duration and installation CAPEX remain unresolved


The ORBIT cable-vessel proxy is treated as a complete lay-spread rate by modelling assumption
Commercial cable-lay cost remains unresolved until the rate boundary is verified


Demobilisation is not generally represented by ORBIT
Complete screening duration remains unresolved until a value is supplied


Survey rates and ROV-support fractions are unresolved
ROV/survey time cannot yet be calculated for a base case


Product section packing and campaign grouping are unresolved
Mass-derived load counts remain lower bounds rather than adopted inventories


The infield example requires about 34 strings while the reference platform has 28 cable bays
The example is conditional on a compatible collector or a redesigned cable topology


Crossing, protection and landfall unit costs are not transferable
Exceptional costs remain site-specific


TCP product, vessel-feasibility, task-time and spread-rate inputs are incomplete
The smaller-vessel pathway is explicit, but TCP spread selection and installation CAPEX remain not parameterized until matching inputs are supplied



The model stops at the highest defensible level for each subclass. It preserves cost-driving physical inventories and discrete logistics while leaving unsupported engineering checks as qualification gates and unresolved cost terms as not parameterized.
Evidence review date: 5 August 2026.

title: Platform and Substation Installation
text:
This page calculates the offshore installation CAPEX of a crane-installed, piled-jacket offshore substation (OSS). Jacket, pile and topside supply are costed separately. The installation result is required to convert those supplied components into an installed and commissioned offshore asset.
The model uses the minimum sufficient detail supported by the available evidence. It represents three installation campaigns:

piled-jacket installation;
topside installation; and
offshore hook-up and commissioning.

Piling and jacket installation are combined because the available public evidence supports their aggregate site duration but not a reliable task-level decomposition. Transport and other campaign logistics are represented by aggregate chargeable days rather than separate carrier schedules.

title: Platform and Substation Installation
text:
Installation-Class Screen
The selected class is rejected when either screening lift mass exceeds its declared capacity:
\[
m_J\leq Q_J,
\qquad
m_{S,\max}\leq Q_S.
\]
This is a one-sided screening check. Failure requires a larger vessel class or another installation method. Passing does not demonstrate lift feasibility: radius, hook height, dynamic effects, lift points, structure clearance, stability, seafastening and weather limits remain part of project lift engineering.
The capacity check preserves the material step between installation classes without introducing unsupported task-level corrections. If the selected class fails, the model reports class change required and does not calculate cost using that class.

title: Platform and Substation Installation
text:
Calculation
The number of topside lifts is
\[
N_S=N_{\mathrm{OSS}}N_{\mathrm{module/OSS}},
\]
where \(N_S\) is a count of lifts. A split topside therefore creates a discrete increase in installation work rather than a smooth mass multiplier.
Chargeable campaign durations are
\[
T_{FJ}=N_{\mathrm{OSS}}t_{FJ}+t_{\mathrm{log},FJ},
\]
\[
T_S=N_St_S+t_{\mathrm{log},S},
\]
\[
T_H=N_{\mathrm{OSS}}t_H.
\]
\(T_{FJ}\), \(T_S\) and \(T_H\) are chargeable days for the complete piled-jacket, topside and hook-up spreads. Mobilisation is costed separately and is therefore not included in these durations.
Normal-scope installation CAPEX is
\[
C_{\mathrm{normal}}
=C_{\mathrm{mob}}
+r_{FJ}T_{FJ}
+r_ST_S
+r_HT_H.
\]
When exceptional work has a defined scope and cost,
\[
C_{\mathrm{inst}}
=C_{\mathrm{normal}}
+C_{\mathrm{exceptional}}.
\]
If exceptional work is relevant but not quantified, it is reported as not included rather than assigned a zero value. Likewise, missing spread rates, mobilisation or hook-up duration block the total cost result; the available campaign durations are still reported.

title: Platform and Substation Installation
text:
Applicability and Limitations
This model applies only to crane-installed topsides on piled jackets. The following cases require another model branch rather than an adjustment factor:

float-over or self-installing topsides;
gravity-base or non-piled foundations;
a failed jacket or topside installation-class screen; and
exceptional work that changes the installation method or campaign structure.

The model deliberately does not calculate pile handling, penetration, crane movement, carrier concurrency, mating or connection time separately. Those details can replace the aggregate parameters later if project evidence shows that the additional fidelity materially improves the estimate.
The current public evidence supports the 5.0 day/OSS piled-jacket and 2.5 day/lift topside anchors (Dominion Energy 2021). It does not support generic complete-spread rates, logistics time or offshore commissioning duration. These remain explicit project inputs rather than inferred assumptions.
Evidence review date: 31 July 2026.

title: Platform Material CAPEX
text:
This page owns the material and fabrication CAPEX of a central offshore platform. The calculation is common to the electricity-export and centralised-hydrogen architectures: architecture-specific equipment determines the hosted mass, and this page converts that physical requirement into the platform structure, its support structure and their cost.
The calculation is a mass chain. Hosted-equipment mass sets the topside mass; the topside mass sets the jacket and pile masses; each mass is multiplied by a unit cost for its own scope. The same masses are passed to Platform and Substation Installation for lift screening.

title: Platform Material CAPEX
text:
Calculation
The calculation is performed per platform and multiplied by \(N_{\mathrm{plat}}\) at the cost step.
Step 1: hosted-equipment mass.
\[
m_{\mathrm{eq}}=\sum_k m_{\mathrm{eq},k}
\]
Step 2: topside mass.
\[
m_{\mathrm{str}}=k_{\mathrm{str}}\,m_{\mathrm{eq}},
\qquad
m_{\mathrm{top}}=m_{\mathrm{eq}}+m_{\mathrm{str}}
\]
\(m_{\mathrm{top}}\) is the complete topside dry mass in tonnes. It is the quantity that \(k_J\) is referenced to.
Step 3: topside lift modules.
\[
N_S=N_{\mathrm{plat}}N_{\mathrm{mod}},
\qquad
m_{S,\max}=\frac{m_{\mathrm{top}}}{N_{\mathrm{mod}}}
\]
The topside is assumed to be split into modules of equal mass. \(N_{\mathrm{mod}}\) is a discrete input, so a split topside is represented as a step in lift count rather than a smooth mass correction.
Step 4: jacket and pile masses.
\[
m_J=k_J\,m_{\mathrm{top}},
\qquad
m_P=a_P\,m_J^{\,b_P}
\]
with \(m_J\) and \(m_P\) in tonnes. \(a_P\) carries the dimension \(\mathrm{t}^{1-b_P}\) implied by the source fit.
Step 5: material and fabrication CAPEX.
\[
C_{\mathrm{str}}=c_{\mathrm{str}}\,m_{\mathrm{str}},
\qquad
C_{\mathrm{int}}=c_{\mathrm{int}}\,m_{\mathrm{eq}},
\qquad
C_J=c_J\,m_J,
\qquad
C_P=\frac{c_P\,e_{2022}}{X}\,m_P
\]
\[
C_{\mathrm{plat}}=N_{\mathrm{plat}}\left(C_{\mathrm{str}}+C_{\mathrm{int}}+C_J+C_P\right)
\]
All terms are in EUR2025. \(C_P\) is escalated in USD before conversion, following the common price basis.
Step 6: averaged specific cost.
\[
c_{\mathrm{plat}}=\frac{C_{\mathrm{plat}}}{P_{\mathrm{plat}}}
\]
\(c_{\mathrm{plat}}\) in EUR2025/kW is a reporting and comparison metric only. The model uses \(C_{\mathrm{plat}}\), which responds to mass, not to rated power.
If any input is unresolved, the corresponding mass or cost is reported as not parameterised rather than zero.

Interface with Installation
This page provides the physical platform definition used by the installation model: \(N_{\mathrm{plat}}\), \(N_S\), \(m_J\), \(m_P\) and \(m_{S,\max}\). The installation page independently checks transport and lift feasibility and calculates vessel occupation and offshore installation CAPEX.

Public reproducibility means that a reader can obtain the cited evidence independently. A controlled source is not independently reproducible merely because its provenance is named.
An unresolved record cannot support a final model result. It remains in the catalog so the missing source or model-use decision stays visible rather than being replaced by an unsupported assumption.

title: Turbine System
text:
The turbine-system model calculates the mass and supply cost of one offshore wind turbine and its monopile foundation. It retains component masses because they connect turbine design to foundation sizing, transport, lifting, and installation-vessel requirements.
The model boundary includes the rotor, nacelle, turbine electrical equipment, tower, monopile, and a transition-piece supply allowance. It excludes offshore transport and installation, scour protection, array infrastructure, export infrastructure, and hydrogen-production equipment. Where architecture-specific equipment is supported by the turbine foundation, its mass is passed into the foundation calculation without moving its cost into the turbine-system boundary.

title: Turbine System
text:
Calculation Dependency
The Turbine Power Electronics page defines the adopted electrical boundary at inverter AC output. The step-up transformer is allocated to electrical infrastructure even when housed in the turbine; the legacy turbine cost ledger still includes it and requires explicit reallocation. Its physical location remains relevant to supported mass and installation.





flowchart LR
  A["Rated capacity, rotor diameter, and hub height"] --> B["Turbine component masses"]
  C["Electrical architecture"] --> B
  B --> D["Complete turbine mass"]
  D --> E["Supported topside mass"]
  F["Additional supported equipment mass"] --> E
  G["Water depth"] --> H["Monopile mass"]
  E --> H
  B --> I["Turbine supply cost"]
  H --> J["Foundation supply cost"]
  D --> K["Transport and installation"]
  H --> K






The foundation model does not use turbine rated power directly. Rated power, rotor diameter, hub height, and electrical architecture first determine the turbine component ledger. The resulting complete turbine mass, including the tower, is then combined with any additional supported equipment and water depth to estimate monopile mass.

title: Wind Turbine Mass and Cost
text:
This page calculates the component masses and supply cost of one offshore wind turbine. The parametric inputs are generator capacity \(P\), rotor diameter \(D\), and hub height \(H_h\). Component masses are retained individually because they determine structural loads, transport requirements, lift configurations, and installation-vessel feasibility.
The calculation uses the NREL Cost and Scaling Model (CSM) implemented in WISDEM. The CSM estimates component masses from high-level turbine inputs and then estimates component costs from those masses (National Renewable Energy Laboratory 2026a). It is used here because its equations and inputs are explicit. WISDEM notes that the regressions include older WindPACT-era relationships and recommends overriding them with more detailed estimates where available (National Renewable Energy Laboratory 2026a).
This implementation is pinned to WISDEM source revision 584c39191b61ab2654c1f1fab2871e0f5bec4064 (National Renewable Energy Laboratory 2026b). A different WISDEM revision must not be substituted without checking every coefficient below.







Included on this page
Accounted elsewhere




Blades, hub, pitch system and spinner
Monopile or other foundation


Mechanical drivetrain and generator
Offshore turbine transport and installation


Nacelle structure and auxiliary systems
Array and export cables


Turbine electrical equipment and transformer when present
Offshore and onshore substations


Tower
Grid connection and other balance-of-system costs



The cost boundary is turbine supply at the stated commercial basis. Offshore transport and installation are calculated on Turbine and Foundation Installation. For decentralised hydrogen, electrolyser, water-treatment, compression, storage, and hydrogen-export equipment are not turbine CAPEX. Their masses must nevertheless enter the installation and structural models when they are installed in or on the turbine.

When hub height is not specified independently, the default relationship provides 15 m lower-tip clearance above mean sea level:
\[
H_h=\frac{D}{2}+15.
\]
The structural tower interface is assumed to be 15 m above mean sea level. Tower length is therefore derived rather than entered independently:
\[
L_t=H_h-15.
\]
Under the default hub-height relationship, \(L_t=D/2\). A project-specific hub height can override the default while retaining the same 15 m interface elevation.

text:
Fixed Model Assumptions
The following quantities are model constants or scenario definitions, not parametric inputs:







Quantity
Baseline treatment




Number of blades
\(n_b=3\)


Maximum blade-tip speed
\(V_\mathrm{tip}=95\) m/s


Rated drivetrain efficiency
\(\eta=0.95\)


Blade regression
IEC Class I with carbon reinforcement


Main bearings
\(n_\mathrm{brg}=2\)


Nacelle crane
Included


Reference drivetrain
Permanent-magnet direct drive


Electrical architecture
Selected scenario: electricity export or decentralised hydrogen



Rated power and rotor diameter do not uniquely determine maximum blade-tip speed. Tip speed is a turbine design and control limit affected by aerodynamic, acoustic, structural, and generator constraints. Fixing it at the IEA 15 MW reference value keeps the parametric model limited to \(P\), \(D\), and \(H_h\) (Gaertner et al. 2020).

title: Wind Turbine Mass and Cost
Wind Turbine Mass and Cost
text:
Rated Speed and Torque
The rated rotor angular velocity follows from the fixed 95 m/s tip-speed limit:
\[
\omega_r=\frac{V_\mathrm{tip}}{D/2}.
\]
Rated rotor speed and low-speed-shaft torque are:
\[
n_r=\omega_r\frac{60}{2\pi},
\qquad
Q_r=\frac{1000P/\eta}{\omega_r},
\]
where \(n_r\) is in revolutions per minute and \(Q_r\) is in Nm. A larger rotor rotates more slowly for the same tip-speed limit and consequently transmits more torque at the same rated power.

title: Wind Turbine Mass and Cost
text:
Rotor Mass

Blade
The baseline WISDEM mass of one blade is:
\[
m_b=0.5\left(\frac{D}{2}\right)^b,
\]
where \(m_b\) is in kg. The exponent \(b\) depends on turbine class and carbon reinforcement (National Renewable Energy Laboratory 2026b).



Blade assumption
\(b\)




Class I with carbon reinforcement
2.47


Class I without carbon reinforcement
2.54


Class II or III with carbon reinforcement
2.44


Class II or III without carbon reinforcement
2.50



The offshore screening case uses Class I with carbon reinforcement unless another class or blade design is specified.


Hub, pitch system, and spinner
Hub mass is:
\[
m_\mathrm{hub}=2.3m_b+1320.
\]
WISDEM first calculates pitch-bearing mass and then complete pitch-system mass:
\[
m_\mathrm{pb}=0.1295n_bm_b+491.31,
\]
\[
m_\mathrm{pitch}=1.328m_\mathrm{pb}+555.
\]
Spinner mass is:
\[
m_\mathrm{spinner}=15.5D-980.
\]
The hub-system and rotor masses are therefore:
\[
m_\mathrm{hubsys}
=m_\mathrm{hub}+m_\mathrm{pitch}+m_\mathrm{spinner},
\]
\[
m_\mathrm{rotor}=n_bm_b+m_\mathrm{hubsys}.
\]
The model retains blade, hub-system, and complete-rotor masses separately so that alternative rotor-assembly and lifting strategies can be evaluated.

title: Wind Turbine Mass and Cost
text:
Nacelle Mass

Low-speed shaft and main bearings
The low-speed-shaft mass is:
\[
m_\mathrm{LSS}
=13\left(m_b\frac{P}{1000}\right)^{0.65}+775.
\]
The mass of one main bearing and the total bearing mass are:
\[
m_\mathrm{bearing}=10^{-4}D^{3.5},
\qquad
m_\mathrm{bearings}=n_\mathrm{brg}m_\mathrm{bearing}.
\]


Gearbox, brake, and high-speed shaft
For a geared drivetrain, the pinned WISDEM source calculates gearbox mass from rated torque:
\[
m_\mathrm{gearbox}=\frac{Q_r}{\rho_Q}.
\]
The source default is \(\rho_Q=200\) Nm/kg. Gearbox mass is zero for direct drive.
Brake and high-speed-shaft masses are:
\[
m_\mathrm{brake}=0.00122Q_r,
\qquad
m_\mathrm{HSS}=0.19894P.
\]
The high-speed shaft is removed for direct drive. Brake mass must be reviewed for the selected direct-drive arrangement rather than retained automatically.


Generator
The simple WISDEM relationship is:
\[
m_\mathrm{generator}=2.3P+3400.
\]
This power-based regression represents a relatively high-speed geared generator. It is not used for a large direct-drive offshore generator, whose mass is governed primarily by rated torque. The direct-drive replacement is defined under Improvements from Mehta.


Nacelle structure and auxiliaries
The remaining WISDEM mass relationships are:
\[
m_\mathrm{bedplate}=D^{2.2},
\]
\[
m_\mathrm{yaw}=1.5\left(0.0009D^{3.314}\right),
\]
\[
m_\mathrm{HVAC}=0.08P,
\]
\[
m_\mathrm{cover}=1.2817P+428.19,
\]
\[
m_\mathrm{platforms}
=0.125m_\mathrm{bedplate}+3000I_\mathrm{crane},
\]
\[
m_\mathrm{transformer}=1.915P+1910.
\]
Transformer mass is included only when a turbine transformer is present in the selected architecture.


Electrical-equipment additions
The CSM does not provide adequate masses for converters, controls, switchgear, internal cabling, DC-link equipment, or electrical protection. Those terms are explicit architecture inputs:
\[
\begin{aligned}
m_\mathrm{electrical}={}&m_\mathrm{converter,GS}
+m_\mathrm{converter,grid}
+m_\mathrm{switchgear}\\
&+m_\mathrm{cabling}
+m_\mathrm{DC-link}
+m_\mathrm{protection},
\end{aligned}
\]
where GS denotes the generator-side converter. A missing required mass remains an unresolved input; it is not silently assigned a value of zero. The direct-DC electrical architecture is developed further on DC Integration.


Nacelle aggregation
Only components present in the selected drivetrain and electrical architecture are included:
\[
\begin{aligned}
m_\mathrm{nacelle}={}&m_\mathrm{LSS}+m_\mathrm{bearings}
+m_\mathrm{gearbox}+m_\mathrm{brake}+m_\mathrm{HSS}\\
&+m_\mathrm{generator}+m_\mathrm{bedplate}+m_\mathrm{yaw}
+m_\mathrm{HVAC}+m_\mathrm{cover}\\
&+m_\mathrm{platforms}+m_\mathrm{transformer}
+m_\mathrm{electrical}.
\end{aligned}
\]

title: Wind Turbine Mass and Cost
text:
Tower Mass
The simple WISDEM tower relationship is:
\[
m_\mathrm{tower}=19.828L_t^{2.0282}.
\]
This regression depends only on tower length. It does not respond to rotor thrust, RNA mass, tower natural-frequency constraints, foundation stiffness, fatigue, or site conditions. It is therefore an initial screening estimate, not the preferred offshore-tower calculation.
TowerSE or an equivalent load-based calculation is required before tower-section masses are used for detailed installation planning. The tower remains inside the turbine-cost boundary; the foundation remains outside it.

title: Wind Turbine Mass and Cost
text:
Aggregate Masses and Installation Outputs
Rotor-nacelle assembly and complete-turbine masses are:
\[
m_\mathrm{RNA}=m_\mathrm{rotor}+m_\mathrm{nacelle},
\]
\[
m_\mathrm{turbine}=m_\mathrm{RNA}+m_\mathrm{tower}.
\]
The calculation passes the following outputs to the installation model:

Largest dimensions and heaviest lift
Vessel and crane feasibility



Tower-section masses and dimensions are not generated by the simple CSM. Until TowerSE is implemented, those installation inputs remain unresolved.

The coefficients are legacy model inputs with mixed evidential ages. They are used to distribute and scale cost between components, not as a current market quotation.
Raw subsystem costs are:
\[
C_\mathrm{rotor,raw}
=n_bC_b+C_\mathrm{hub}+C_\mathrm{pitch}+C_\mathrm{spinner},
\]
\[
C_\mathrm{nacelle,raw}=\sum_{i\in\mathrm{nacelle}}C_i,
\]
\[
C_\mathrm{turbine,raw}
=C_\mathrm{rotor,raw}+C_\mathrm{nacelle,raw}+C_\mathrm{tower,raw}.
\]
WISDEM permits assembly, overhead, profit, and transport multipliers. Their defaults are zero (National Renewable Energy Laboratory 2026a). Offshore transport remains excluded on this page. Assembly, overhead, profit, and warranty must either be stated as separate supply-cost adders or included through the calibration below.

title: Wind Turbine Mass and Cost
Wind Turbine Mass and Cost
text:
Decentralised Hydrogen Architecture
The decentralised-hydrogen turbine is represented by changing the component ledger. No general percentage reduction is applied to turbine mass or cost.
For architecture \(a\):
\[
m_{\mathrm{nacelle},a}
=\sum_i x_{i,a}m_i+\sum_jm_{j,a}^{\mathrm{replacement}},
\]
\[
C_{\mathrm{turbine},a}
=\sum_i x_{i,a}C_i+\sum_jC_{j,a}^{\mathrm{replacement}},
\]
where \(x_{i,a}=1\) when component \(i\) is present and zero when it is absent.
A conventional electricity-export turbine may contain a generator-side converter or rectifier, DC link, grid-side inverter, step-up transformer, AC switchgear, protection, and high-voltage internal cabling. A direct-DC hydrogen turbine may remove or resize the grid-side inverter, transformer, part of the AC switchgear, and part of the high-voltage cabling. It may require replacement DC-link, DC protection, DC-DC conversion, cooling, and structural equipment.
The mass and cost changes are therefore:
\[
\Delta m_\mathrm{H2}
=m_\mathrm{removed}-m_\mathrm{replacement}+m_\mathrm{reinforcement},
\]
\[
\Delta C_\mathrm{H2}
=C_\mathrm{removed}-C_\mathrm{replacement}+C_\mathrm{reinforcement}.
\]
WISDEM calculates transformer mass explicitly. Converter, switchgear, protection, and cabling masses require separate evidence. A lighter nacelle may also reduce tower and foundation mass, but that secondary effect cannot be calculated with the length-only WISDEM tower regression.

Electrical removal credit
The adopted turbine electrical boundary excludes the step-up transformer from turbine supply cost and places the power-curve boundary at the inverter AC output. The equations and executable calibration on this page still describe the legacy package including its transformer. Its calibrated transformer term must be reallocated to electrical infrastructure without changing the combined AC package cost. Physical transformer mass remains in the applicable support and lifting inventory. The following adjustment describes the current implementation pending that migration, not a second transformer purchase.
The model keeps the conventional turbine as the common baseline for every architecture and applies turbine-level changes through the per-turbine input turbine-electrical-cost-adjustment. Its scope follows the shared inventory on Power Conversion Equipment:



Item
Treatment in the adjustment




Step-up transformer
Removed in both turbine-level cases. The credit can follow the explicit, calibrated WISDEM transformer term in this ledger; its scope is the transformer only


Grid-side inverter
Removed in both turbine-level cases, but no credit is claimed: the calibrated cost has no separable converter term, and no public source prices the grid-side half of a converter package


Generator-side converter and DC link
Retained in every case; no adjustment


Stack-side DC/DC converter
Not in this adjustment; booked through the turbine-level conversion unit cost on DC Integration


DC protection, switchgear and cabling changes
Enter the adjustment only with explicit evidence



The adjustment remains blank until these terms are evidenced and normalised to EUR2025. No blanket percentage of turbine cost is removed.

title: Wind Turbine Mass and Cost
text:
Improvements from Mehta
Mehta, Zaaijer, and von Terzi scale turbine properties around the direct-drive IEA 15 MW reference turbine (Mehta et al. 2024; Gaertner et al. 2020). Their complete model is not substituted for WISDEM: the paper does not publish standalone equations for every component, and its absolute turbine-cost calibration is not adopted. Four relationships nevertheless improve identifiable weaknesses in the WISDEM baseline.

1. Load-responsive blade mass
WISDEM blade mass depends on \(D\) but does not respond to the higher rated wind speed and thrust associated with greater specific power. Mehta introduces:
\[
m_b
=m_{b,\mathrm{ref}}
\left(\frac{D}{D_\mathrm{ref}}\right)^\beta
\left(\frac{V_r}{V_{r,\mathrm{ref}}}\right)^2,
\]
with baseline \(\beta=3\). Rated wind speed is calculated from:
\[
V_r
=\left(
\frac{1000P}
{\tfrac{1}{2}\rho A C_{P,\max}\eta}
\right)^{1/3},
\qquad
A=\frac{\pi D^2}{4}.
\]
This relationship should replace the WISDEM blade-mass regression when the model varies both \(P\) and \(D\) around the IEA 15 MW design. Hub, pitch, and spinner masses remain separate WISDEM components. The exponent \(\beta\) is an uncertainty input because geometric cubic scaling does not represent every future blade technology.


2. Mixed blade-cost scaling
WISDEM makes blade cost proportional to blade mass. Mehta separates material-related cost from tooling, labour, and other diameter-related costs:
\[
C_b
=\gamma_\mathrm{mass}C_{b,\mathrm{ref}}
\frac{m_b}{m_{b,\mathrm{ref}}}
+(1-\gamma_\mathrm{mass})C_{b,\mathrm{ref}}
\left(\frac{D}{D_\mathrm{ref}}\right)^\alpha.
\]
The baseline parameters are \(\gamma_\mathrm{mass}=0.6\) and \(\alpha=2\) (Mehta et al. 2024). This replaces only the blade cost relationship. The absolute reference blade cost must come from the adopted NREL-compatible calibration; Mehta’s absolute reference cost is not used.


3. Torque-based direct-drive generator
For a permanent-magnet direct-drive turbine, generator mass is scaled with rated torque:
\[
m_\mathrm{generator}
=m_\mathrm{generator,ref}
\frac{Q_r}{Q_{r,\mathrm{ref}}}.
\]
The archived Mehta implementation uses \(m_\mathrm{generator,ref}=372{,}000\) kg and \(Q_{r,\mathrm{ref}}=20.308\) MNm (Mehta 2023). This corresponds to a reference torque density of approximately 54.6 Nm/kg. The relationship replaces the WISDEM power-based generator equation for direct drive. Generator torque density remains an uncertainty parameter because electromagnetic architecture, structural support, and cooling can change it materially.


4. Tower feedback
Mehta scales hub height linearly from the IEA 15 MW reference. That relationship is not adopted here because the model instead uses the directly interpretable lower-tip-clearance relationship \(H_h=D/2+15\). A project-specific hub height can override this default.
Mehta’s support-structure method nevertheless demonstrates that tower mass must respond to RNA mass, rotor thrust, hub height, and site conditions. The full coupled monopile calculation is outside the turbine boundary, so the intended improvement is TowerSE rather than importing Mehta’s complete support-structure module.

title: Wind Turbine Mass and Cost
text:
Model Status and Limitations
The implemented hierarchy is:

WISDEM provides the component ledger and baseline mass equations.
Mehta replaces blade mass and blade cost when both capacity and rotor diameter vary.
Mehta’s torque relationship replaces the WISDEM generator equation for direct drive.
Architecture-specific component inputs represent conventional electricity export and decentralised hydrogen.
Separate RNA and tower factors calibrate raw WISDEM costs to NREL.
All component masses pass to the later installation calculation.

The calculation remains incomplete for detailed design until converter, switchgear, internal-cabling, and DC-interface masses are sourced and a load-based tower calculation produces tower-section geometry. These missing inputs are exposed explicitly. The model is a transparent scaling model, not a certified turbine design or supplier quotation, and is most reliable near the scale and architecture of its reference turbine.

title: Wind Turbine Mass and Cost
section: Worked Example: 15 MW Turbine with a 236 m Rotor
text:
Worked Example: 15 MW Turbine with a 236 m Rotor
This example evaluates a conventional electricity-export turbine with:
\[
P=15{,}000\ \mathrm{kW},
\qquad
D=236\ \mathrm{m}.
\]
The default hub-height and tower-length relationships give:
\[
H_h=\frac{236}{2}+15=133\ \mathrm{m},
\]
\[
L_t=H_h-15=118\ \mathrm{m}.
\]
The fixed assumptions are three blades, 95 m/s maximum tip speed, 95% drivetrain efficiency, two main bearings, a nacelle crane, and a permanent-magnet direct-drive generator. Mehta’s load-responsive relationship is used for blade mass and its torque relationship is used for generator mass. The remaining applicable component masses follow the pinned WISDEM equations.

Converter, switchgear, DC-link, protection, and internal-cabling masses are not included because no traceable mass inputs have yet been selected. The nacelle, RNA, and complete-turbine results are therefore known-component subtotals. They must be updated before use as final transport or lifting masses.


Cost calibration
The raw WISDEM component costs are calibrated to NREL’s 12 MW offshore reference. The NREL reference uses \(P_\mathrm{ref}=\) 12000 kW, \(D_\mathrm{ref}=\) 216 m, \(H_{h,\mathrm{ref}}=\) 137 m, RNA cost of 1462 USD/kW, and tower cost of 238 USD/kW (Stehly et al. 2023).
The raw blade-cost anchor is the WISDEM coefficient applied to the 65 t IEA 15 MW reference blade:
\[
C_{b,\mathrm{ref,raw}}
=14.6\times65{,}000
=949{,}000\ \mathrm{USD/blade}.
\]
This anchor is used in Mehta’s mixed mass/non-mass blade-cost relationship for both the NREL calibration turbine and the 236 m example. The subsequent RNA calibration, rather than the raw blade anchor, sets the absolute turbine cost level.
At the NREL reference geometry, the model gives raw RNA and tower costs of USD 10.232 million and USD 0.980 million. The published calibration totals are:
\[
C_\mathrm{RNA,ref}^{\mathrm{NREL}}
=12{,}000\times1{,}462
=17.544\ \mathrm{million\ USD},
\]
\[
C_\mathrm{tower,ref}^{\mathrm{NREL}}
=12{,}000\times238
=2.856\ \mathrm{million\ USD}.
\]
The resulting factors are:
\[
k_\mathrm{RNA}=1.7146,
\qquad
k_\mathrm{tower}=2.9142.
\]
The RNA factor is applied to every raw rotor and nacelle cost. The tower factor is applied only to the raw tower cost. This preserves the component-level WISDEM scaling while reproducing the separate NREL RNA and tower reference costs.

title: Wake Modelling and Spacing
text:
This calculation turns turbine coordinates, a tabulated turbine curve and a set of wind states into the wake-affected electrical power of every turbine in every state. That table is the common input to all architectures: it gives power at the generator electrical output, before any architecture-specific conversion or collection loss. The implementation is calculate_wakes in model/wind_resource_and_layout/wake_modelling_and_spacing.py.
The layout is deliberately schematic. It exposes the relationship between installed capacity, occupied area, turbine separation and wake loss without claiming to reproduce a consented or commercially optimised wind-farm layout.

title: Wake Modelling and Spacing
text:
Layout
A scenario supplies coordinates directly, or declares a regular grid (turbine count, columns, spacings and rotation) whose incomplete final row is centred. In both cases the model checks that every pair of turbines is at least the declared minimum separation apart and rejects the layout otherwise. Farm area is a reporting boundary; it is never used as a multiplier on distances.
The article reference case generates its coordinates from the agreed site record: a rectangle across the dominant wind direction, rows numbered from the upwind edge and an explicit rotation convention (see the reference case).

title: Wake Modelling and Spacing
text:
Turbine Performance
The wake calculation uses a supplied, tabulated power and thrust-coefficient curve; it never builds a synthetic curve. The article case uses the pinned IEA 15 MW reference turbine release (Gaertner et al. 2020; IEA Wind TCP Task 37 2026), whose power column is electrical output. Zero power and thrust are declared just outside the operating range, because PyWake would otherwise hold the first tabulated value for waked turbines below cut-in.

title: Wake Modelling and Spacing
text:
Wake Calculation
PyWake evaluates every state with the following configuration (DTU Wind and Energy Systems 2026):








Model element
Selection
Function




Site
UniformSite with ambient \(I_0\)
Uniform inflow; state weights come from the wind-state table, not from the site


Propagation
PropagateDownwind
Calculates wakes from upstream to downstream turbines


Wake deficit
TurboNOJDeficit
Turbulence-dependent top-hat wake expansion (Nygaard et al. 2020)


Rotor averaging
AreaOverlapAvgModel, on the deficit model
Partial overlap of a top-hat wake and a downstream rotor


Superposition
SquaredSum
Combines deficits from several upstream turbines


Blockage
None
Upstream induction is excluded



The calculation is run once per wind direction for all speeds in that direction; each state keeps its own speed and weight. For state \(s\) and turbine \(j\) the result is the wake-affected power \(P_{j,s}\) in kW. The installed PyWake version is recorded with each result.

title: Wake Modelling and Spacing
text:
Annual Energy and Outputs
The wake-affected and no-wake annual energies, in MWh/year, are
\[
E_\mathrm{wake}=\frac{1}{1000}\sum_s h_s\sum_j P_{j,s},
\qquad
E_0=\frac{N}{1000}\sum_s h_s\,P(v_s),
\]
and the wake loss and wake-affected gross capacity factor are
\[
L_\mathrm{wake}=1-\frac{E_\mathrm{wake}}{E_0},
\qquad
CF_\mathrm{wake,gross}=\frac{1000\,E_\mathrm{wake}}{NP_r\,\sum_s h_s}.
\]
These exclude availability, collection, conversion and export losses, which are applied downstream and must not be applied again here. For the article reference case the result is a wake loss of 10.0% and a gross capacity factor of 54.7%.
The model accepts the wind input in two equivalent forms: a wind-state table with a turbine curve, from which it runs PyWake itself (optional wind dependency), or a stored table of per-turbine power by state. The article case stores the table, generated with the same function by research_articles/turbine_level_hydrogen/analysis/prepare_common_case.py, so that both architectures read identical turbine power and a case run does not need PyWake. A zero-hour design state may be added for peak-duty sizing.

title: Wake Modelling and Spacing
text:
Legacy Implementation
The earlier model used a synthetic ramp-shaped power curve with a constant thrust coefficient, PyWake’s UniformWeibullSite with sector-edge directions, a fixed 30° orientation and a grid truncated after \(N\) positions. These are replaced by the method above and are retained only for traceability of older results.






WarningRemaining improvements




Benchmark the wake model. Compare representative dense and sparse layouts against at least one credible alternative wake formulation and use the difference as model uncertainty.
Test turbulence and blockage sensitivity. The provisional \(I_0\) directly affects TurboNOJDeficit; evaluate a sourced range and quantify whether the omission of blockage changes the comparison.
Source the minimum-separation check. The article case keeps the unsourced legacy threshold of three rotor diameters as a coordinate check only.



Higher-fidelity CFD, LES and full commercial layout optimisation are not proposed at this stage. They are justified only if the simpler model has first been made internally consistent and the remaining wake uncertainty can materially change the comparison.
